1.	Is it true that the inmates in the Kingston penitentiary, of whom 30 per cent are French speaking, are not given the right, or the privilege, of listening to a French speaking channel over their radio system, in their cells?
2.	If so, does the government intend to correct this situation?
3.	Does the same situation exist in the other penitentiary institutions in Canada?

1.	No. The Kingston penitentiary cellular radio system relays broadcasts on two nets with a two net receiver located in each cell. One of these nets relays French broadcasts

on the basis of two hours per day. The other net is used almost entirely for sports programming.
The radio system programming is governed by the wishes of the inmate population and reflects such wishes on a proportionate basis.
It should be noted that French radio broadcasting is not available in Kingston city, nor in the immediate geographical area. The reception of such broadcasting presents technical difficulties, since it originates from Cornwall, Hull or Montreal, and the quality of sound reception varies from time to time.
2.	Yes. Equipment and material have been requisitioned to provide a third net with a view to providing more extensive French radio reception.
3.	Yes. A similar situation exists at Dorchester penitentiary where French programs are broadcast on the basis of one hour per day, in accordance with the wishes of the inmate population, as expressed by the institutional inmates' recreation committee which includes French representation.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: U.S. ORDER RESPECTING INSPECTION OF BANKS IN FOREIGN COUNTRIES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a number of questions to the Minister of Finance in connection with an order of the federal reserve board of the United States which permits United States government inspection of banks controlled by United States banks outside that country. In view of this, is it the intention of the government to reexamine the sale of shares of Canadian banks to United States banks? Has any reply been received to the protest, if any, Which has been made to the United States in respect of an order which extends the authority of the United States government beyond its territorial boundaries? I should also like to ask the minister whether he will table the terms of the Canadian objection and the United States reply so that Canadians may know, not second hand but directly, what is the attitude of the government of Canada in this connection.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: U.S. ORDER RESPECTING INSPECTION OF BANKS IN FOREIGN COUNTRIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I reply to the first of these questions and then ask my colleague the Secretary of State for External Affairs to reply to the remainder.

It is not the intention of the government to ask for any further revisions to the Bank Act as a result of the regulation of the federal reserve board of the United States. subsubtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to participate in this debate which centres around a budget which many hon. members have said had no real purposes and was really unnecessary because the money to be raised by the $300 million tax increase imposed upon the citizens of Canada purportedly to pay the increase in pensions to senior citizens, establishing what has become known as the basic wage for senior citizens, was already available in the old age security fund and will still be in that fund when the pension increase takes effect on March 1. It was really shameful for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) to make the senior citizens of Canada the goat for this tax increase. It is something which was resented and will be resented in the years ahead by our senior citizens.
The financial year 1966-67 will go down in history as a very interesting one. Canadians will remember two things in particular about it. It will long be remembered as a year in which the country had a great deal of labour difficulty and a great many strikes. It will also long be remembered as a year in which Canadians saw their country suffer many financial difficulties. These two major difficulties, labour strife and financial strife, are the direct responsibility of the government because of the actions it took.
We are debating a budget which increases taxes and the cost of living and is a backward attempt to put the brakes on inflation. Some of the most interesting comments on the budget were made in a C.B.C. "Viewpoint" telecast by a Montreal Star newspaper reporter. He said that as a result of the budget 2,300,000 Canadians will pay higher income taxes. He added:
A married couple just getting going on less than $100 a week will pay more on income.
A man struggling to keep a wife and four children on $120 will pay more on his income.
And every Canadian will pay more in sales taxes. Nobody escapes.
He wound up by saying:
If this is a mini-budget, heaven deliver us from a maxi-budget.
In essence the budget was too severe. It was unnecessary and it was shameful of the minister to blame our senior citizens for the tax increase. To analyse the budget fully one must go back to 1963 when the government took office. Even though the Liberal party was a minority in the house it formed the government and its immediate aim was to call another election and get a majority. How was
12954	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. J. H. Horner this to be accomplished. Members of the government had to create the impression of a boom in Canada. Most economists agree that our economy started to boom back in 1961. However, the boom was not increasing fast enough for members of the government and so they decided to create an excessive boom.
The government immediately set to work to double the money supply. The total money supply in Canada today has increased very nearly 50 per cent over what it was in 1963. In fact I have a letter from a minister in which he states quite frankly that the government made a deliberate decision to increase the money supply. Such an increase in the money supply could only result in inflation, and there is no need for me to repeat the story of that inflation. Citizen's groups all across Canada have been writing to members of parliament complaining about inflation and 1966 will long be remembered for the tremendous increase. In actual fact the inflation was ignited by the too rapid increase in money supply as a result of the deliberate decision of the government, and it has been perpetuated by the government's action in granting huge wage increases to a number of labour unions without any regard for the effects these wage increases would have on the unions themselves and on all citizens. One might wonder how they could do so many things and not really affect the economy of the country.

I think this is one reason we became involved in a great many financial difficulties in 1966. One financial house closed down and others barely stayed alive as the result of huge loans by the government. One need only take a look at the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation report for 1965 in which the following statement appears:
Under section 11 of the National Housing Act, holders of N.H.A. mortgages may be provided with a source of short-term credit if required. Ten loans were made under this provision of the act in 1965, representing the first activity under this particular section of the housing legislation.
In other words, this is the first time the government has lent money to financial houses. They did so because they feared the collapse of a whole series of financial houses after the failure of Atlantic Acceptance Corporation. They bailed out some of these companies by making loans available. The report states further:
The loans were approved late in the year as a result of the difficult conditions in the mortgage market which prevailed at the time. The loans amounted to $29.9 million on which the balance owing at year-end was $24.4 million.

It became very difficult to ascertain the names of the ten companies. The government was very sensitive about this point. One can hardly blame them, because if the information became public knowledge perhaps more finance companies would be in difficulty since no doubt money would be withdrawn and they surely would collapse.
Why did the finance companies find themselves in danger? Because of the oversupply of money which caused inflation. Then there was a severe clamping down on the money circulating throughout the economy resulting in a tight-money situation. To a large extent this is what caused the financial houses to be in difficulty. In some cases, mind you, there were other things which had a greater effect, but this is the reason ten houses in particular were in difficulty. First of all, there was the government's announcement that the bank interest rate would be increased. Perhaps they thought this would be a curb on inflation. In these days when there is so much money being borrowed by everyone action of this type tends to create more inflation because the people who borrow money continue to borrow even at the higher rates and the result is that the goods produced cost more.
We find Canada getting into a great deal of difficulty in respect of banking. We saw the Mercantile Bank get into difficulty because all of a sudden the government decided it must place restrictions on a foreign-owned bank. Many people forget the fact that the Mercantile Bank was completely foreign-owned when First National City Bank of New York bought it. It was owned by Dutch interests. When the Dutch concern applied for a charter in 1949 we had a Liberal government. The government did not tell them that if they did receive a charter they must allow Canadians to participate in their company. Rather than say that the government simply hoped that this bank would remain small and not become too much of an influence.
I would be the first to say that we should have absolute control over our banking system. The error was made in 1949 when the Mercantile Bank was first given its charter. It never said it was going to become Canadian. It asked for and was granted a Canadian charter. When the original owners of the Mercantile Bank decided to pull out the government should have said "All right, set your price and we will buy you out; we will put the bank in trust and sell it to Canadians". After all, this is the party which has been advocating the setting up of the Canada

Development Corporation. How better could a development corporation start than by having a bank charter? This is one of the positive steps the government could have taken which would have bailed it out of a lot of trouble. But no. After a series of manipulations and meetings at which notes were made on pieces of paper by individuals the government said, "We hope you will not buy". They should have been firm at that time. If the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Gordon), the minister of finance at that time, really thought that Canadian banks should belong to Canadians he should have said to the owners of Mercantile, "If you do sell we want the privilege of meeting the price and buying the bank". This is what should have been done. It was not done.
Finally, after the bank is sold to the First National City Bank retroactive legislation is brought in to curb it. In other words, as soon as the bank, which was in Dutch hands, is sold to a United States concern the government steps in and limits the expansion of the bank in Canada. Retroactive discrimination is the only term which can be applied to this legislation. The government is not yet out of the mess.
Last week there was some concern over the newly granted charter of the Bank of Western Canada. Mr. Coyne came marching down to Ottawa to tell the finance committee and the house what the trouble was all about. It was all nonsense. When Mr. Coyne brought the matter before the committee on finance, trade and economic affairs he knew the facts and he knew exactly what would happen. But for some reason or other Mr. Coyne believed that Mr. Stevens wanted to get rid of him and he said, "No, you are not firing me, or if you do I will cause you trouble". Apparently Mr. Coyne is good at causing trouble when someone wants to fire him.
I think the interesting thing to note is that the government knew Mr. Stevens' finance companies were in difficulty at the time they granted the charter to the Bank of Western Canada. The government knew this. I defy the Minister of Finance to stand up in the house and say that none of the companies owned by Mr. Stevens' syndicate is among the ten companies mentioned in the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation report that the government bailed out. Some of them definitely are. I think I can safely say two were or perhaps five. The government knew. That is the point which is most interesting.

It was logical to expect that the charter would bail out those few companies. It is interesting to note this article concerning Mr. Coyne in the Winnipeg Tribune of Thursday, April 28, 1966. The article is headed "Coyne Gets Keel-hauled" and reads in part as follows:
James E. Coyne, former governor of the Bank of Canada, encountered some sharp criticism of his investing judgment on Wednesday.
That has to do with one of the questions which was involved when the charter of the Bank of Western Canada was being obtained. The article continues:
Mr. Coyne confirmed that $1.5 million of N.H.A. mortgages had been purchased from Fort Garry Trust and $1 million from York Trust and Savings Corp. of Toronto. I have the floor. The minister can make a detailed explanation in respect of his action regarding that charter when I am finished.
We in this house all know how these charters come about and how private members' bills are sponsored in the house. The minister can sit there and say that the government had nothing to do with it, but we all know what the situation was. One can look up the facts and find that on July 4 of last year the charter was granted to the Bank of Western Canada. During the last month when the bill was being debated the government moved it to the top of the order paper day after day. The minister may well say he knows nothing about that, but that was done time after time with the consent of the government because it wanted to see this group given a charter. I can only guess why, but it certainly was not


intended to improve the position of western Canada.
During the committee meetings I asked Mr. Coyne why he wanted a charter for the Bank of Western Canada and he pointed out that he wanted to help that area. I asked him what particular industries he was interested in helping in a financial way and he said he had not studied the matter to that extent.
At the same time I asked Mr. Coyne if that area of Canada could be considered a surplus depository area and he answered in the affirmative. I found it difficult to believe that until he presented the facts. I then asked the Inspector General of Banks whether or not he would agree that western Canada was an area one could call a surplus depository area, and he said yes.
Under these circumstances what do we end up with in western Canada? I suggest we have a new bank operating in a surplus depository area in order to assist some 14 financial investment houses operating in Ontatio, with 53 per cent of the shares held by three men living in Toronto. Most of these financial houses were in difficulty at that time, and the minister, whether he likes to or not, must accept full responsibility for granting this charter. He can sit there and say that parliament granted the charter but he knew then as he does now the ten companies associated with the B. I. F. group.
Mr. Coyne was completely aware of the situation as indicated by the article which appeared in the Winnipeg Tribune on April 28. There is no doubt in my mind that the government also knew of the situation and, having known, it should have stepped in to prevent this group from getting a charter. The government should have refused to issue the charter even after parliament passed the private member's bill. Perhaps the government felt it owed Mr. Coyne a special favour. I can only surmise what the factors were, which is a dangerous thing to do without knowing the facts. One must do the best one can without the facts. I tried to find out the names of the ten companies involved in the B. I. F. group but I could only find out two.
It is my felling that the trouble in which Canada now finds itself in respect of financing has resulted from poor management on the part of the Liberal government. This government has handled the financial affairs of the country very badly. We all realize that our money supply must be increased, but the government increased the supply too rapidly and then followed that rapid increase with a too severe and lengthy tight-money period.
February 13, 1967	COMMONS
The government must accept responsibility for the difficult financial circumstances which now exist because of its attitude toward labour problems. It has set a precedent by allowing a 33 per cent wage increase to certain workers, as a result of which other labour unions are attempting to obtain similar increases. It is all well and good for the government to suggest that Canadians should invest more in Canada, but how can they expect Canadians to invest more when their confidence has been so badly shaken in the past year? One would have to use a pretty big stick to make Canadians invest in Canadian investment companies because of the government's mishandling of our financial difficulties. The government must bear the burden of its mismanagement in this our centennial year. For the sake of Canada and Canadians I hope the government will do a better job of dealing with labour problems, inflation and financial institutions in 1967, than it did in 1966.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would not want to miss this opportunity to say a few words about the minibudget brought down in the house by the Minister of Finance and Receiver General (Mr. Sharp). It is probably the first one in our history to impose new taxes on the people to get money for the old age security fund.
Before examining closely all the statements made by the Minister of Finance and Receiver General, I would like first to set out clearly the four basic principles which guide us, the Creditistes of Canada. I see that the minister is in his seat. He is an intelligent man, since he presides over Canada's financial future and I feel that he will easily understand the four basic principles which guide us, the Creditistes in our country, Canada.
Here are those four principles. First:

Social Credit firmly believes that the individual is the most important factor in organized society. Because he is a divinely created being with spiritual, mental and physical needs and potentialities, he has inalienable rights which must be respected and preserved. Because of this belief Social Credit is inalterably opposed to communism, fascism and all forms of totalitarian government which make the individual citizen subservient to the state. It stands opposed to political organization whose aims are the furtherance of the sectional interests of organized labour, business, or finance.
The Budget-Mr. Caouette [Translation]
The following is the second basic principle which guides us in our work:

Government must serve the individual. The major function of democratic government in organized society is to secure for the people the results they want from the management of their public affairs, as far as such results are physically possible and morally right.

I think the hon. Minister of Finance will agree with us that the essential task of a democratic government in an organized society is to serve the people and to try to obtain the results which the people expect of the government, in so far as these results are physically possible.
The third basic principle of the Creditistes is this:

The individual must be free and have economic security. The individual can only attain his full stature in a society where his ability to make moral choices is restricted as little as possible. Economic security is a necessary means for attaining this freedom not as an end to be attained by restricting it.

This is the fourth basic principle:

The physically possible must be regarded as the financially possible. Whatever is physically possible, desirable, and morally right, can and should be made financially possible.

Those, Mr. Speaker, are the four basic principles of the Creditistes. The hon. Minister of Finance often tells us, as he did a while ago, that a bank charter, for instance, is granted by parliament and not by the government. He said a few minutes ago, speaking of the Western Bank of Canada, that parliament granted the charter and that the government had nothing to do with it.
Mr. Speaker, I maintain that though the Canadian people are told that parliament decides, we know, here in the house, that the government decides, because the party line must be followed. It is understood that the Liberals on the government side will vote for the government when the time comes to grant a bank charter. As the government has the majority in the house, government decides and not parliament.
Parliament should decide, parliament should be free to decide important issues such as granting bank charters in Canada,
February 13, 1967

The Budget-Mr. Caouette but that is not the case. The government has always decided, whether it was the present, the former or any of the successive governments, ever since confederation. In fact, we have had instances where the members of the government rose to speak in favour of increased old age pensions, but who voted against the amendment to increase them proposed by the opposition. Why? Because party discipline required that they vote against their convictions, because the matter became a political game.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. Minister of Finance takes pleasure in often repeating: We, of the federal government, have only two ways of finding money: loans and taxes. As I see it, there could be a third way: inflation. Those are the answers of the hon. Minister of Finance. Third way: inflation. But the only two ways the government can find money are through loans and taxes.
I say there are other ways of finding money and credit. The minister of Finance and Receiver General knows quite well that money and credit do not grow on spruce or on fir trees, whether in Lotbiniere or Vil-leneuve ridings. That is not where they grow.
Money and credit originate somewhere. But where? This the Minister of Finance and Receiver General never explains. He never mentions the creators of credit and money, never. He always answers: there are only two means at our disposal: borrowing and levying taxes. But before borrowing and taxing, the money had to originate somewhere. Where? The provinces do not create money and credit, they do and say what the federal government does and says, we borrow and we levy taxes. The municipal authorities and school boards say: we borrow and we levy taxes.
And the federal government, the central government, the supreme government gives us the same answer: we borrow and we levy taxes. These are our only ways of creating money and credit.
While the house is in session I sometimes attend sittings of the committee on finance, trade and economic affairs where we are given the opportunity to question presidents of various banks, the governor of the Bank of Canada and others. These people admit that $8 enables them to create $100 worth of credit, that they are authorized to give as much expansion to the Canadian credit as they wish, but we must pay interest on this credit.

I believe it was to a Bank of Nova Scotia economist that I once said this: When the federal government issues or buys $1 million worth of bonds, the Canadian chartered banks are immediately authorized by law and by charter to grant loans totalling $12.5 million.
Mr. Speaker, where does that credit come from? From the pen and the ink stand. Twelve million and a half. Would it not be as easy for the government to use the Bank of Canada and to tell it to create those twelve and a half million for the benefit of the Canadian people, instead of giving that power to a few individuals who control the economic lifeblood of the nation and who crush, as they see fit, industry, private enterprise and even the government because, in many cases, the latter is obliged to kowtow to those controllers who dispense credit as they please, with the blessing of the federal government.
We are not the only ones to ask for the use of the means available to us to appreciate the assets of our country, to make the development of our natural resources possible, to avoid the chaos which results from inflation and deflation. The means are available to us, and parliament has the power to decide and to legislate.
We do not use the powers available to us. We prefer to grant special licenses to individuals so as to let them exploit all the people.
The Minister of Finance and Receiver General knows fully well that parliament has the right to give orders to the Bank of Canada under section 91 of the B.N.A. Act. It is the prerogative, the right of the federal parliament to legislate in money matters. The provinces do not have that right. Then, why does not the federal government allow the provinces, the school boards, the municipalities, to cope-not with the possibilities of physical expansion-but with the financial possibilities to do so. Ask the provinces, the municipalities, the school boards what is their problem?
At the present time, in the province of Quebec, thousands of teachers are at loggerheads with school boards and the provincial government. Why those recriminations, those discussions and such an alarming situation in the province of Quebec? The question of finance. The school boards do not have enough funds to meet their obligations under their budget at present. Increased expenses are required, which they cannot meet.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
On the other hand, the teachers are entitled to better treatment, they have a right to
February 13, 1967	COMMONS
recognition. But if we look at the situation at present in Quebec, I say this is complete anarchy, because they do not put the Anger on the cause of the evil, because they are afraid to touch the system which has placed the school boards in the position where they are at present, which has placed the government in its present dilemma, which has put municipalities in their present state of stagnation. Why? Because we have been using for one hundred years a debt-money system.
The cost of building a school is doubled, because of the interest required. The cost of building a road is doubled, because of the interest to be paid. The cost of building a city hall is doubled when the interest to be paid is included.
But the value of a city hall is never doubled; on the contrary, every year the building depreciates in value. A road has never been worth twice the amount it cost. Now, to double the cost of such public services is to resort to inAation 100 per cent, because over a period of 20 years you have to pay back double the amount of the capital borrowed originally.
This system may still not worry some of the people, but I can assure you that it is coming to an end. When school children are throwing tomatoes and rotten eggs at their teachers, when teachers are up in arms against school trustees, when school trustees are up in arms against the government, in short, when one sees what is going on in some places across the country, I think it is high time for a responsible government to set the Anancial system in order.
Otherwise our children will pay the piper and will never forgive us for not having taken proper steps at the proper time.
I am not the only one requesting that the Anancial system be set in order, I know that among Liberals-I see my hon. friend from Matapedia-Matane (Mr. Tremblay) who is an expert in this Aeld and knows that the Anancial system is faulty, that it needs to be improved and amended. He knows that the Bank of Canada should be used, instead of encouraging and granting to a few individuals the right to exercise Anancial control right across Canada. He knows that.
Some members of the Conservative and N.D.P. parties know it too. The parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance knows that the Bank of Canada could be used, if a decision was taken to that effect. Such a decision could be taken under our constitution.
The Budget-Mr. Caouette
We are not facing up to our responsibilities, and when we know-I will quote again today-

speechtext:
I am. To bring some people to reason sometimes one has to repeat oneself over and over again, continuously.
Now, I want to quote three presidents of the United States who were up against the problem we are facing today. Here is what Thomas Jefferson said, and I quote:

I believe the banking institutions are more dangerous to our liberties than standing armies.

Mr. Speaker, Thomas Jefferson was not a stupid man nor a moron. He knew what he was talking about.

Already they have raised up a moneyed aristocracy that has set the government at defiance. The issuing power should be taken from the banks and restored to the people to whom it properly belongs.

That is what a former president of the United States had to say, and to reach that station in life, or to become president of the United States, it seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that one has to use one's head, at least a little.
In 1829-not in 1967-John Adams made some remarks that, in my opinion, could very well be applied to the situation that exists in Canada in 1967. I quote:

Ail the perplexities, confusion and distress in America arise, not from defects in their constitution or confederation; not from want of honor or virtue, so much as from downright ignorance of the nature of coin, credit and circulation.

Mr. Speaker, when one considers those who object to confederation or the constitution, in short, the citizens of the east who attack westerners, French Canadians who blame Englishmen and Englishmen who blame French Canadians, one may wonder what will be the effect of such an attitude on our Anan-cial system.
The constitution is not faulty. When we examine sections 91, 92, 93 and 94a of the constitution, we become aware of the fact that each province enjoys exactly the same privileges and rights. But we do not know
February 13, 1967

The Budget-Mr. Caouette them and we are fighting within confederation against confederation. We accuse others and blame them for what we have not had the courage to do ourselves; we attack everybody, except those who are really responsible, because we are not yet convinced in 1967 of our-
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)

-downright ignorance of the nature of coin, credit and circulation.

There lies the essence of the problem. As soon as we decide to set things right we will see that no one is afraid of confederation; neither I nor the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette) will lie awake at the propsect of a visit to Canada by Her Majesty the Queen, that is for sure; she can come if she wants to. We will show her respect; to us she will represent those who at least permitted us to become what we are today. She will be that much to us, and we will discover the cause of the present faults in our responsible financial system.
As for the financiers, their great motto is simple: Divide and rule. It does not matter whether we have separatists, co-separatists, separatists to a greater degree, to lesser degree, fanatics in other areas, Anglo-Saxon fanatics, or what have you. As long as we remain divided one against the other, with as many groups as possible, right and left, finance will remain master.
It is not the Queen of England who rules in Canada, it is the financial system.
We may say Her Majesty the Queen, yes, but "the power behind the throne" is stronger than that, Mr. Speaker. There you have the all powerful master.
When Abraham Lincoln, another one-time president of the United States said:

I have two great enemies-the southern army in front of me, and the financial institutions in the rear.

He said: The financial institutions behind and the southern army ahead. The army, he could see. Those behind, he could not see, he could feel them.

Of the two, the one behind is my greatest foe.


Lincoln said: Of those two enemies I have, the most dangerous, the one which is the most troublesome, is the group of financiers who are behind me. As a matter of fact, to win the war, he had at one time to issue what were called greenbacks, and that enabled him to pay his soldiers without having to call on the financial institutions. But they caught up with him later on, because he did not have the support of the American Congress, because he did not have the support of the government. But if the government had the support of a parliament like ours, to get high finance to toe the line, it would be as easy as passing the act to increase old age pensions in this country.
And Lincoln said:

The government should create, issue and circulate all the currency required to satisfy the spending power of the government and the buying power of consumers. The privilege of creating and issuing money is not only the supreme prerogative of government, it is the government's greatest creative opportunity.

That was Lincoln speaking.

The people can and will be furnished with a currency as safe as their own country. Money will cease to be master and become the servant of the people. Democracy will rise superior to the money power.

That is precisely what the Creditistes are asking for. Not an unlimited financial credit or monetary creation. Not flood the country with greenbacks, as we say, or paper money, but create credit up to the exact amount of the existing resources in Canada. That is all we are asking for. Put things in order, set a balance between the purchasing power and the goods and services produced by the Canadian people.
Is there a sensible economist who can pass by this logical and plausible solution? [English]
Money will cease to be master and become the servant of the people. Democracy will rise superior to the money power.

That is what the members of the Creditistes request, Mr. Speaker.
February 13, 1967

And at this point, we might quote other bankers who, tor their part, defy governments:

The chairman of the United States Federal Reserve Board, Marriner J. Eccles, said:
The banks can create and destroy money; bank credit is money. It is money we do most of our business with, not with that currency which we usually think of as money.

It is so true that 95 per cent of the business in Canada, at the present time, is transacted by transfers of figures from one bank account to another. Figures only, for which there is not a nickel in circulation. Five per cent only of Canadian business is transacted with paper money or with hard cash, money in the pocket as we say in good French, while 95 per cent is done by transfers of figures from one account to another. And where are those figures created? In the government? No, the figures are created by the Canadian chartered banks. That is where.
The value of a bond can be created, as I said earlier. The government issues its bond series for one million, the Bank of Canada buys it for one million. But as soon as the Bank of Canada has bought it for a million, immediately, the reserve of the chartered banks increases and, that way they can multiply by 12 and a half times the initial amount of one million, which clearly allows a credit production of $12.5 million which are going to be loaned later on to the government at a rate of 4J, 4J, 5, 5| per cent. But the government will quench its thirst, will feed itself out of the hands of those people to whom we gave the right in Canada to create millions and billions practically without restriction. Mr. Eccles said:

It is money we do most of our business with, not with that currency which we usually think of as money.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)

Another banker, Mr. Mayer-Anselme Rothschild, said:

Let me issue the money of a nation and I care not who makes its laws.

It is exactly that. When the Minister of Finance and Receiver General tells us: "We have only two ways at our disposal to find

The Budget-Mr. Caouette money: loans and taxes", it means that he has to admit what Mr. Rothschild said once:

Let me issue the money of the nation and I care not who makes its laws.

Those people are above the law, and we realize this in the committee on finance, trade and economic affairs, the meetings of which we attend. We ask questions but receive replies that are not too precise. We ask them whether they create credit and they answer as follows: No, we do not create credit, we only "expand" credit.

It is a credit expansion, it is not the creation of money. It is just the expansion of credit.

What is the difference between expansion and creation, in the circumstances? Mr. Graham Towers, former governor of the Bank of Canada said the following and he is an expert in banking affairs:

That is the banking business (creating money), just the same way that a steel plant makes steel. Now, if parliament wants to change the form of operating the banking system, then certainly that is within the power of parliament.

That is precisely what I was saying a while ago, that parliament has the right to change this banking system, to amend it, to improve it. This does not mean cancelling all bank accounts and eliminating chartered banks in Canada. No. Let us keep the chartered banks, in order to finance the private sector of our economy. It is all very well, Mr. Speaker, for a businessman, a manufacturer to get credit from chartered banks, but when it comes to public capital, our municipalities, our school boards, our provincial government-

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I will not take advantage of my colleagues' generosity. I shall be brief.
To conclude, I want to say this: We believe that the government should use the Bank of Canada to finance the public sector of our economy. Our provinces, our municipalities, our school boards should have the right to borrow from the Bank of Canada, in a branch of the Bank of Canada, in any province, without interest, because they are public, nonprofitable organizations. We have no objection to those public organizations being able to finance themselves from the source of credit of the Bank of Canada, without interest, and to the private sector continuing to use the money which chartered banks are in a position to provide, for the smooth running of their business.
We do not want to nationalize anyone, but we believe that it is time for the government and parliament to use the Bank of Canada not only as a mainspring to give more power to the chartered banks but also to use it as a national institution which will help the economic development of our country and enable us to develop confederation in unity of all who inhabit Canada, including the French Canadians in Quebec as well as the Ukrainians in Manitoba and the Englishmen in Toronto or Vancouver.
Mr. Speaker, that is where the trouble lies. That is where we should bring a solution to help us make Canada the greatest country in the world, where life is good, the best country where there is agreement, where people do not tear each other apart but co-operate in its expansion.

I quite agree that this has been a productive session, Mr. Speaker, but I am trying to make our sessions more productive. Unless we have some acceptance of this principle we are not going to be able to meet the heavy obligations that face the government with regard to its legislation and which deny us, I think regrettably, the opportunity for fuller discussion on matters of serious concern to Canada in its relations with other countries, and particularly on some of the major problems that concern all nations in the world at this time.
As a result, Mr. Speaker, there are people who say that they are not aware of what Canadian policy is on Viet Nam. I certainly believe that we should encourage the right of discussion, and equally the right of dissent. What those who say that they do not understand Canadian policy really mean, of course, is that they do not agree with this policy. Canadian policy on Viet Nam involves efforts by this country and certain other countries to help bring the war in Viet Nam to an end.
Now, Mr. Speaker, obviously there is room for disagreement about what our policy is. I do not ask everyone to accept that policy, but I do ask the house and the country to understand the circumstances in which foreign policy here or elsewhere must be conducted, particularly when vital issues are involved, issues that affect the peace of the world.
I believe that much of the criticism of the Canadian government's policy in this area is based on the unrealistic view that Canada is in a position to compel acceptance of its analysis of the Viet Nam situation. We are not a combatant power. We are a member of an international supervisory and control organization that has been in existence for 12 years. Yet much of the criticism levelled against us, and not only against us but against Poland, India and certain other countries, almost seems to presuppose that these
February 13, 1967

countries have some direct responsibility for this regrettable conflict.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, I welcome discussion. I am not concerned about the criticism. I am concerned, as I said to the students of McGill University on Friday last, that there be understanding of the role that Canada is seeking to play in this very difficult and important question.
I ask, Mr. Speaker, what is it open to Canada to do in this conflict? What has Canada in fact been trying to do? First of all, we have tried to form the best possible judgment of the position of the parties to the conflict. We are in a good position to do this because of the close relationship we have, first of all, with our neighbour the United States, and also because of the access which we, among very few countries, have to Hanoi as a result of our membership on the International Control Commission. This gives us the opportunity not only to make reasonably informed judgments but to keep abreast of the evolution of the positions of both sides.
Second, Mr. Speaker, we can try to devise formulas which stand some chance of bridging the gap which still separates the positions of the two sides. This we have been doing, and so have other countries. It is not always possible, because of the very nature of the situation, to disclose all that we are doing, and particularly if we wish to enjoy the confidence of those who are prepared to use our good offices. The real problem is not the dearth of such formulas but the complexity of the problem to which they must be addressed. What is at issue here is not Canadian influence or initiative but the urgent need to find a way out of the present impasse which both sides can accept as not being incompatible with their real interests.
[DOT] (4:40 p.ra.)
Third, we can try in common with our other partners on the International Control Commission, as we are doing and as we have been doing for 11 months, to make the instrumentality of the commission available to the parties when the circumstances are right. We believe that the circumstances may now be ripening. I would like to think that our two colleague states will come to agree with that judgment in the light of events during the past few days. But the commission is powerless to compel the parties to do what they are not prepared to do on their own account. All that the commission can do is provide an umbrella which, when the time comes, may enable them to take certain steps
The Budget-Hon. P. Martin and allow certain steps to be taken which in any other context they might find it difficult to contemplate.
I may be asked: what are those steps? But if I say that I cannot indicate what those steps are I shall perhaps be accused of evasion. I do not mind the accusation, but I can only say that if I do not state them it is because we have made commitments-I hope no one will say commitments to the United States only-to the parties involved in this matter which, if violated, would in my opinion mean that our future efforts would not be respected or trusted.
I believe there is a valid distinction to be drawn between the role of the individual in this kind of situation and the role of a government. The possibilities open to an individual for constructive political action are different from those open to a government. Individuals do not have the responsibility of discharging foreign policy and cannot, naturally, be made fully aware of all the facts. In a democracy there must never be a denial of discussion of commitments the government makes in its relations with other states. Before policy is finally decided, parliament and the public certainly have a right to know. But in matters of negotiation, particularly when questions of war and peace are involved, it cannot be expected that a government should on every occasion make disclosures which are not in the best interests of achieving the objectives we all have in mind.
In the final analysis it must be the foreign minister who makes the decision with the support of his colleagues. I am prepared to make it. I will not change in any way the course I have pursued in this matter because my primary aim, and that of the government, has been to enable Canada along with other countries to try to bring an end to the war in Viet Nam.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It will not be brought to an end by engaging in wild denunciation. The house must not expect me to take such a course and then to enjoy the confidence of both sides. Lose that confidence, and anything we might do or attempt to do would be destroyed.
There are those who urge us to speak out against this or that aspect of the war. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) asked me the other day whether I would agree that this house should pass a resolution condemning the bombing in the north or that
February 13, 1967

The Budget-Hon. P. Martin we should pass a resolution urging that the bombing in the north be brought to an end. I ask the house to reflect. If I had given an immediate, positive response, what would have been the consequence? What would have been the consequence for whatever service this country might perform in an intermediary capacity, either alone or collectively with other nations? I do not question for a moment the sincerity or the sense of urgency Which lies behind these demands, and I take no exception to whatever hon. members of this house may urge me to do today. But I would ask the advocates of political activism to pause for a moment and reflect on the practical consequences of their proposal. Do they believe that if a government-and I mean the Canadian government-made a series of strong public declarations the basis of its Viet Nam policy, the tangled and dangerous problem in that country would begin to unravel itself?
To be more specific, let us look at the question of the bombing of North Viet Nam. I have said already that this may be the key to the whole problem. I am confident that if it is not the key element in the present military-diplomatic puzzle it is certainly a most important factor. There are other factors. Even though I hope the bombing does stop, there are other actions and responsibilities which must also be fitted into the total pattern of steps toward a peaceful settlement. Until at least some faint outline of a pattern can be established through what has been called quiet diplomacy, it seems unlikely that the bombing would stop for a long period simply in response to a Canadian government demand or appeal, regardless of what individual Canadians or members of the government personally might feel about this aspect of the policy of the United States.
I suggest it would be self-defeating if our public statements, no matter how widely acclaimed they might be in this house and this country, were to have the effect of slamming doors instead of opening them, or closing off potentially useful dialogues instead of stimulating and nurturing the confidential exchange of view points. I ask members of this house, who can influence these matters by their pronouncements and by their deliberations, to appreciate the significance of what I am saying. What government in the free world has taken any other course? Under what foreign minister, in Britain, for example, under a Labour government, or in any country except France, has there been a lack of restraint in

criticism against the policy of a particular country?
In one of his despatches from Hanoi Mr. Harrison Salisbury of the New York Times formulated the following prescription on the basis of his conversations there. He said:
What is needed are not headlines, publicized missions, pressures or formulas but the quiet and painstaking uses of the old-fashioned confidential techniques of the pre-electronic era.
9 (4:50 p.m.)
I subscribe to that view. As long as I hold this particular portfolio that will be the course I will pursue. I am convinced it is the right one.
Canada does occupy a special position in Viet Nam because for 12 years, along with India and Poland, it has shared in the frustrating experiences of service on the international commission. It enjoys, as no other institution does, contact with both sides and reflects by its composition a wide variety of international opinion. The efforts of the commission in the war situation have had minimal results but that is not because we have not tried. The commission cannot impose its will on the United States, on North Viet Nam, on South Viet Nam, on China or on the Soviet Union. It may not be the instrument that will be finally used to promote agreement but it is our duty, as Canada sees it, to be ready for the slightest opportunity to achieve that end and, who knows, that opportunity may not necessarily be far away. I cannot say so positively, but I feel there are elements in the present situation that might cause India, Poland and Canada to recognize that there may be a special role for them in the Viet Nam situation as it is now unfolding.
I took the view last March that, if we could not get an understanding with Poland and India as to the time when the commission should be used according to our proposals- and these were discussed privately and confidentially in Warsaw and in Delhi-then we should try ourselves. It was with that objective that on two occasions Mr. Chester Ron-ning, as a representative of the government of Canada, was sent to Hanoi to carry on certain conversations with the government of North Viet Nam.
I can say this, and I can confirm it as of recent days, that the channel which was thus established is still open. Perhaps it was this channel, amongst others, that Mr. Rusk had in mind in his press conference last Thursday. I am not saying this is the only channel, but it remains open. For that reason I resented the publicity given to a groundless report that
February 13, 1967

Mr. Chester Ronning's services would no longer be used by the government because he had exercised the right to express private opinions, no longer being a permanent member of the Department of External Affairs. There was no foundation for that story. We can use that channel or the mechanism of the commission, depending on the circumstances.
I am often asked in the house, what did Mr. Ronning say in Hanoi, what went on there? I am often asked what was said in the discussions which took place a few weeks ago when Mr. Victor Moore went there, indeed, what took place last fall when Mr. Victor Moore was in Hanoi, and because I do not give a forthcoming reply I am charged with evasion. I do not mind the charge, but I am asking for an understanding by this house and by the country as to why I cannot say more at the present time.
Mr. Ronning, in anything he has said publicly, has not disclosed the detail of his conversations in Hanoi. Naturally we want to enjoy the confidence of all sides and to do that we must respect commitments which we have made to all sides. Other countries have tried their best, sometimes with one side. We have tried our best with both sides and we will continue to do so.
I believe that it would be helpful if the Canadian position on a settlement of the Viet Nam conflict were restated so that those most directly concerned, particularly in Asia, would know precisely where Canada stands.
First, we believe that a military solution alone is neither practicable nor desirable. We have always made it clear the we look to negotiation to settle this conflict. We have said this because we think that the Viet Nam situation cannot be isolated from the security and stability of southeast Asia as a whole. We have not been alone in saying this. If there is to be a settlement which will hold out a reasonable prospect of long-term stability in that area of southeast Asia it will have to be based upon an accommodation of the interests of those primarily concerned. I do not believe this will happen as the result of military action alone.
Second, peace discussions should take place on the basis of the Geneva agreement. We believe that, without any prejudice whatsoever to the ultimate solutions, the first stage of any settlement will have to envisage a return to the status quo ante. By that we mean the conditions which were envisaged as ensuing from the Geneva ceasefire agreement of 1954. According to my understanding the government of North Viet Nam does not take issue
The Budget-Hon. P. Martin with that position. In practice this involves a continuing of the de facto division into two Viet Nams, if only to allow time for the scars which have been opened by the conflicts of the past quarter century to heal and for new dispositions to be agreed upon for the eventual reunification of the country.
Third, we recognize the unity of the people of Viet Nam. We have no wish to inhibit the reunification of Viet Nam. We are bound to recognize, however, that the temporary division of that country reflects the political realities of the situation and cannot be abrogated by force. It is for the people in the two parts of Viet Nam to decide how soon and under what conditions preparations for reunification can be set in train. This is not something which can be imposed upon the people of Viet Nam from the outside or in disregard of the principle which they must enjoy, like anyone else, of self-determination.
Fourth, we believe that any Viet Nam settlement will have to involve an international presence. We believe it is generally agreed that as soon as conditions permit there must be a withdrawal of all outside forces from both parts of Viet Nam. This would be consistent with the terms of the Geneva agreement. The same applies to military bases maintained in Viet Nam.
We believe that it is likely to be necessary, for some period at any rate, to have international supervision of any settlement agreed to by the parties. The purpose of such supervision would be to give each side adequate guarantees that the terms of such a settlement were being fairly carried out. We have no firm views as to what form that international supervision might take.
If it were decided that the three powers represented on the present international commission should assume a new mandate in an expanded form, I can assure the house that Canada would be prepared to co-operate fully in the constitution of a new supervisory force. In that event we shall have to consider, in the light of our experience, what powers and what resources should be given to such a force if it is to carry out its mandate effectively and with the best interests of the parties in mind, c (5:00 p.m.)
Fifth, we believe that it is for the Vietnamese people themselves to determine their own political future and the shape of the institutions under which they wish to live. We welcome the progress which has been made in South Viet Nam to bring about the conditions
February 13, 1967

The Budget-Hon. P. Martin in which a constitutional government, responsive to the interests of the people of the south, can be elected. We understand that this process will be completed within the current year. We would hope, when the hostilities have ceased and a settlement of the current conflict has been reached, that all segments of the people of South Viet Nam will be afforded an opportunity to participate on a fair, constitutional and peaceful basis in the political life of South Viet Nam, but so far as the representation of the Viet Cong at a conference is concerned, in the words of Mr. Goldberg's recent statement, this did not seem to present an insurmountable problem.
Sixth, we can see merit in proposals which have been made for the neutralization not only of Viet Nam but of a wider area in southeast Asia.
Seventh, we believe that in southeast Asia, as in other parts of the developing world, there is a close link between the requirements of stability and the requirements of economic development.
I would hope, Mr. Speaker, that the governments of North and South Viet Nam would take note of this statement of our view concerning the nature of a possible peace settlement. I would hope they would regard it as an earnest of our desire to help bring about an end to the war in Viet Nam.
There are many things with which I should like to have dealt on this very subject, but there will be an opportunity when the external affairs committee meets.
One question is addressed to me from many quarters: How can you say that you are pursuing the objective of peace when instruments of destruction manufactured in this country find their way into Viet Nam? The Prime Minister dealt with this question on January 18. I should like to supplement what he said by pointing out that we have a defence production sharing agreement with our great and friendly neighbour. This agreement was formulated in 1959. At that time it was warmly approved by every section of the house and was endorsed by the people of Canada.
The fact is that although there may be illogicalities, the government of Canada does not itself authorize the shipment of arms made in this country direct to any theatre of war. I know the answer that will be given to what I am saying now. In general it will be said that we must know that military equipment sold by Canada to the United States may find its way to Viet Nam. I will not try to
IMr. Martin (Essex East).]
dodge what is obvious, but I do ask those who make this argument to do it in fairness and with a sense of the circumstances in which this situation has developed.
I could say something now about what other countries on the other side are doing. I could say something right now about what some countries who do not support our point of view and who give strong support to Hanoi are doing by way of direct assistance. I could do that and I could enumerate the items. But if I were to do that, then I would have to ask myself how that would help with those with whom we are engaged at the present time in trying to bring about a basis for preliminary talks.
Mr. Speaker, I have restated some of Canada's positions with regard to the war in Viet Nam and outlined the principles which we believe should apply if and when peace is achieved in that regrettably divided country. I say to members of the house, not because I want sympathy but because I want to assure them that the government is not in any way relenting in its efforts, that there is no problem before the department over which I preside which during the past year has engaged more of our attention, more of the energies of our personnel, and which has brought us into contact more closely with Poland and India as well as with the governments of the south and the north and the government of the United States, than has this question.
When the time comes to give to this house and to this country the record of what we have been trying to do I will be content to let the record speak for itself. I have been in politics a long time. I know as well as any man in this house the art of debate. I know what people can do by way of rhetorical questioning, and I received a lot of this the other day at McGill University.

with my own profession, my own conduct in public life, and my own training in public life.
I can only assure this house, on behalf of the government, that we will do our utmost to help bring to an end a conflict which we have not started and in which we are not engaged but the solution to which we regard as indispensable for building a more orderly world. I believe we are in the throes of great achievement in the international community. I look forward shortly to signing for Canada a nonproliferation agreement in respect of nuclear weapons, an agreement which I hope will take into account the position of those countries whose nuclear capacity is dedicated to peaceful purposes and who must receive some guarantees and some assurances if they too are not to join the nuclear club.
We have just signed the agreement to outlaw nuclear weapons in outer space. These things are all part of a tremendous achievement which demonstrates the easing of international tension that is taking place between east and west in spite of the fact that the uncertain state of things in China must cause us all concern. The visit of Mr. Kosygin to Britain the other day, his being received by the Queen and speaking to the British parliament, are indications of what is happening. I ask this house to believe that with the influence at our disposal we are doing all we can to bring peace to the people of Viet Nam.

Mr. Speaker, I have a limited amount of time in which to speak. It was not my intention to speak on the subject of Viet Nam. We had no notice that the Secretary of

State for External Affairs was going to make a statement. I say very clearly that we did not have time before he spoke, while he was speaking or since to adopt what might be called an official position on behalf of our party, but I think the things I have said represent our views. While I do not ordinarily mind questions, I would like in the time I have left to deal with the subject which I intended to discuss. Therefore I would appreciate not being asked any more questions on the subject of Viet Nam.
The mini-budget which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) presented to the house some weeks ago, like the budget he presented early in 1966, seems to me to have one main purpose, namely, to slow down those programs outlined by the government itself in earlier years and during election campaigns. We have had a postponement of the date for implementing medicare. We have had a disastrous slowdown in housing starts which has led to increasing hardship for people both in the low and medium income groups in regard to finding adequate housing. This hardship has been described in detail by a newspaper as close to the government as the Toronto Star as a "major disaster".
We have had the complete ignoring of the solemn pledge made by the government during several election campaigns that the Liberal party, if returned to office, would implement a program of 10,000 university scholarships. That program has gone with the wind and I suppose it will not reappear until 1968 or 1969 when an election is forthcoming, or perhaps not even until some time in the 1970's if the Liberal party thinks this kind of proposal will get it votes at that time.
It is my intention today to speak about the kind of programs which are being ignored by the Minister of Finance and are of basic importance to this country. I refer to programs for the fostering of education and scientific research, without which this country cannot meet the needs of the 1970's. The Economic Council of Canada dealt with this important question in their second annual review issued in December, 1965, when they said:
To advance educational levels through the formal education system, attention currently needs to be focused on five particular areas.
I refer to the fourth point which they make:
The more rapid development of facilities for a sharply accelerating flow of professional and other highly skilled manpower at the postgraduate university level-the level at which we have made least progress to date in the Canadian educational system.
The Budget-Mr. Orlikow
In the same report they give some very interesting statistics in comparing Canada with the United States. If hon. members will look at page 84 of the report they will see that in terms of the percentage of the male labour force, only 4.2 per cent of Canadians in the year 1960 had a university degree compared with 7.2 per cent of the male labour force of the United States. That kind of thing is a disaster for this country. What it has meant is that we have had and continue to have a very serious exodus of the most highly trained, most highly skilled people from Canada to the United States.
In the year 1965, according to figures supplied in answer to a question which I put on the order paper, 242 scientists, 863 engineers, 133 professors and instructors, and 380 physicians and surgeons left this country for the United States. It has been claimed by some that this is not very serious, that what we lose to the United States we make up by people coming to Canada from Europe. One of the organizations best able to judge this question, the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, issued in 1966 a special report on the subject of the loss of scientists and engineers to the United States. I wish to quote from a summary of that report which appeared in the Toronto Globe and Mail of April 13, 1966. The article reads:
The O.E.C.D. Observer, In a special issue on science, calculated that the average annual loss of scientists and engineers to the United States was G62 for Britain, 425 for West Germany, 136 for the Netherlands, and 82 for France. The Canadian annual loss was 1,239-almost equal to the combined total of 1,305 for the four major countries of western Europe.
They go into the reasons for this and say:
In relation to output, U.S. spending on research and development was equal to 3.1 per cent of gross national product in 1962. The figure was 2.2 per cent for Britain, 1.8 per cent for the Netherlands, 1.5 per cent for France, 1.3 per cent for Germany, and 1 per cent for Belgium.
The O.E.C.D. did not calculate a figure for Canada, but Ottawa authorities have estimated that research and development spending in 1963 was running at about 1 per cent of gross national product.
Is it any wonder that Canadian scientists, professors, doctors and engineers leave this country for the United States? The Dominion Bureau of Statistics, in a publication it issues annually entitled "Federal Government Expenditures On Scientific Activities" reports that for the year 1965-66 Canadian government expenditures for scientific research totalled $396 million. I want to compare this figure with that for the United States. To do

Congress has held the National Science Foundation budget to a trifle under $480 million... In fiscal 1966, for example, NSF awarded 3647 research grants; in the current fiscal year the number was 3600: next year, if NSF gets the money, it is seeking, it plans to award 3870 . .. These figures do not include the now separately budgeted National Institute of Mental Health, for which expenditures are budgeted to rise from the current nearly $200 million to $257 million.
One of the reasons, according to some people, why we have not been able to do the job in the field of research is that the constitution of Canada leaves education to the provinces.
Professor J. A. Corry, principal of Queen's University, in a speech which he made some time ago and which was printed in the December, 1966 issue of University Affairs, dealt with this matter quite effectively, I think, when he said:
But, It will be asked, does not section 93 of the British North America Act give exclusive power over education to the provinces? This is correct, subject to a limitation that is likely to become more portentous as time goes on. Literally, the words of section 93 are "In and for each province, the legislature may exclusively make laws in relation to education". If there are national needs and objectives that require concerted educational policy in two, several, or all provinces, no provincial legislature is by itself competent in the matter, and judicial interpretation oh other comparable aspects of the distribution of powers under the British North America Act makes it clear that parliament is competent, under "the peace order and good government" clause.
That the provinces would agree to an increased expenditure on the part of the federal government in the field of scientific research is made obvious in the recent report according to which the province of Quebec is proposing to build a $28 million research centre in the field of electrical problems and in the fact that Mr. Johnson, the premier of Quebec, has expressed the hope that the federal government will participate in the financing of that research project. If the province of Quebec is ready to agree to the participation of the federal government I am certain that no other province would object. It seems to

me that this government should have faced up to the problem by now.
Two or three years ago we set up with a good deal of fanfare the scientific secretariat headed by Dr. Forward. If I am critical it is certainly not of the scientific secretariat because I am sure that the staff of that secretariat is very competent. This year the announcement was made, with still more publicity and fanfare, of the establishment of a science council the membership of which is made up of some of the ablest and most respected scientists in this country. However, what can the scientific secretariat and the science council do if the government of Canada is not prepared, and it has not been prepared to this day, to do more than go through the gesture of increasing support for scientific research?
I referred earlier to the fact that the amount of the gross national product which this country is devoting to scientific research is less than a third of the amount which the United States is devoting for the same purpose, The situation is even worse than those figures would indicate because while they refer to what the governments are doing the fact is that Canadian industry spends on research only a fraction of what United States industry does. In a report on the establishment of the science council which appeared in Science magazine.-and I believe it is a very fair report of what is happening in Canada- this very subject is dealt with, namely, the fact that Canadian industry does not spend the money and does not have the kind of research programs which United States industry has. I wish to read a paragraph dealing with this subject which appeared in Science magazine dated September 2, 1966:
Much of the explanation for industry's inferior position vis-a-vis the government in matters of research lies in the peculiar nature of the Canadian economy. For a variety of reasons Canadian industry has been slow to undertake ambitious R & D programs on its own initiative, although this is no longer as true as it once was. Firms oriented to Canada's small, protected, internal market often have had neither the resources nor the incentive to do research. The branch plants and subsidiaries of American and other foreign companies, which dominate some major industries, frequently have looked to their parent companies for R & D work.
It is true that in the last couple of years we have improved our position somewhat through tax incentives and direct grants, but in relation to the problem as a whole and to the tremendous role which scientific research should be playing in this country what we have done is virtually nothing. I want to
February 13, 1967

document the charge I have made by referring to a report submitted to the Bladen commission dealing with research by the committee on research of McGill University. I want to read a few paragraphs from this very excellent report. Here is what it says about the biological sciences:
While comparatively well-supported, these sciences are in fact not given the support they should have, and their strength is comparative only. Canada is not putting enough money and effort into research and therefore all the areas of endeavour are under-supplied. In the case of the biological sciences, the main concern at present is the loss of American funds due to the change of policy whereby research funds are to be spent within the United States rather than outside it.
I want to remind hon. members and bring it to the attention of the public that Canada is spending for medical research not one-tenth of what the United States spends, which we should do since our population is one-tenth that of the United States, but only one-hundredth of what that country spends. Therefore it is not surprising that every year, for the last ten years 100 or more of our best doctors and best medical researchers have left Canada to go to the United States. It is surprising not that they go but that more have not gone.
In the same report the McGill committee writes about the physical sciences and says:
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
The physical sciences are in a worse plight, both comparatively and absolutely. The cost of sophisticated equipment is now becoming such that a scientist being invited to join a university staff will often detail his equipment and funding needs as a condition of his acceptance. The shortage of staff in the physical science departments, due in part to the opening of new universities, the drain to the States, and the continual movement into industry, put the chairmen of these departments into a most unenviable position.
In the few minutes I have left, Mr. Speaker, I want to deal with the problem of medical research, a problem which has been dealt with by a number of other speakers in this debate. It is a problem about which I and other members have spoken on a number of occasions, a problem which the government seems determined to ignore and one which has led within the last year to four of the 12 medical colleges in this country being threatened with loss of their accreditation. The names of the schools involved have not been made public. Steps were taken to assure that they would not lose their accreditation. Some money was made available. In fact, however, the position of these medical colleges is now precarious.
The Budget-Mr. Orlikow
A report was presented to the government more than a year ago, which was prepared by Mr. Gundy of Wood, Gundy and Company. I understand the firm is really associated with the firm Woods, Gordon, a name which has some status in this house.

The parliamentary secretary says I am wrong but the letterhead seems to indicate this. In any case the report signed by Mr. Gundy was prepared after consultation with, and the assistance of, competent and experienced medical researchers in this country. It is a report which ought to make every member of this house hang his head in shame. Yet, Mr. Speaker, so far as I can find out it is a report which has been virtually ignored by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp), the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson).
I should like to summarize, in the few minutes I have left, some of the comments made in this report:
We wish to emphasize that a substantial increase in support for medical research is needed at once. There is an alternative view, that time is required to bring about an expansion of physical facilties, and in well-qualified staff and research of merit. While this view has substance, it overlooks the major injury which would be caused to medical research in Canada unless an immediate indication is given of a greatly improved level of support.
This report was made 15 month ago, but there has been no indication from the government of the support requested. I continue quoting:
Unless a more favourable environment for medical research is provided as a matter of urgency, the skilled manpower on which all else depends will be inadequate both in quantity and in quality to bring about the longer-term expansion needed.
The report has some very interesting tables. For the year 1965-66, the funds available for medical research from various sources totalled $21.5 million, of which $1.5 million came from the United States. This was $7.5 million less than the amount requested by the people involved in medical research. I want to emphasize that medical researchers, having had lots of experience in dealing with this government, had already pared their requests to the bone.

I hope I have made my case in a factual way. What I have said with regard to scientific research is not the view of this party alone. What I have said, I am convinced, represents the views and desires of people who are involved in scientific research, who realize the tremendous importance to Canada of expanding what we have done, who realize that unless we do these things now Canada will rapidly become a second class country.
