speechtext:
I can well forgive the hon. member's narrow view. I have listened to him in the committee and I know what little contribution he has made. He understands the problem about which I am talking as thoroughly as a grade 1 student would.
I should like to deal now with another matter which in my view has been neglected. I refer to the question of unemployment. I was a backbench member of the party in office during the years 1962-63 and I well remember how that paragon of virtue now Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) used to pop up almost daily and ask my hon. friend who was minister of labour at that time what he planned to do about the serious unemployment situation-well over 400,000 men were unemployed, he said. This happened day in and day out until the hon. gentleman had "sold" to the Canadian people the idea that the employment situation was really drastic.
I have before me the bulletin issued by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics on February 9. I commend this to the hon. member who does not agree with my opinions with regard to immigration. There are more than 521,000 people unemployed in Canada today, representing more than 5.2 per cent of the labour force. No government can be proud of such a record. I believe the Liberal government is

misleading Canadians in its definition of unemployment and employment and that, equally, it is misrepresenting the employment figures derived from the Dominion Bureau of Statistics in a way which I can only describe as politically calculated reporting and analysing.
I want to substantiate my argument by placing on record part of an article which appeared in the Toronto Telegram recently under the name of Peter C. Whitehouse, a very competent newspaperman. The heading is "Unemployment: An Economic Blight". He writes:
Canada's misleading definition of employment and the equally misleading employment figures derived from it obscure an unconscionable economic blight -the underemployment and unemployment of huge numbers of men over the age of 45.
Those are not my words. They were written by a competent newspaperman, broadcaster and writer whose specialties include science, politics and economics. He goes on to say:
Some of the 450,000 to 500,000 men 45-64 out of work due to age are included in the 140,000 men of 45-64 the government officially classes as "not in the labour force." Some are in the 61,000 classed as unemployed, and some in various groups such as the 15,000 men classed as not working for "miscellaneous reasons."
But it seems definite that the majority are hidden away in the hundreds of thousands of men who work only a few hours or days a week, and yet are falsely classed as "employed."
Mr. Whitehouse deals with the "safe age". He says:
The problem of over-age unemployment isn't one that starts at 45, and that until that age a man is "safe." Age begins to be an obstacle long before 45. Government figures show that 43.6 per cent of all jobs are closed to men of 35, and a study of the newspapers will reveal that many employers set 27 or 28 as their maximum age for hiring.
Forty-five, however, is the watershed, the age at which, if a man leaves his job (or as is so often the case today, his job leaves him) he has virtually no chance of ever working again.
[DOT] (6:10 p.m.)
We stress retraining, and we litter executives' desks with propaganda saying that existing staff and older people should be retrained. We also stress that new immigrants coming into the country must be skilled people trained for specific jobs. Is it not our responsibility first to create a situation where we can provide 50,000 or 500,000 new jobs and then lay emphasis on retraining and on admission to Canada by reason solely of skills? This is one of the reasons why I feel that government policy today in this area is totally inadequate.
February 13, 19S7

When one reads present unemployment statistics one must agree that the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury) cannot be held blameless. For instance, it was not too long ago that General Motors laid off a number of men for a given period of time. Only last month, January, Chrysler in Windsor laid off some 5,000 workers which resulted in a production decrease of 2,900 cars. Something other than the infamous Canada-U.S. automotive agreement has to be brought to the fore before we can adequately look after the unemployed who are walking the streets of our cities.
Although I am sure the Minister of Finance has read it, I wish to quote an article from the Toronto Telegram, reprinted in the Edmonton Journal of February 8, on a speech delivered by Mr. J. A. Coates, a Toronto lawyer who was a member of the Carter royal commission on taxation. These are some of the suggestions he made, and I commend them to the minister:
A consideration that could give our ailing home building industry a shot in the arm is the deductibility of interest expense on mortgage loans. "It's generally agreed that interest makes up about half the amount of most mortgage payments."
He also suggests:
Exemption of tax on state and municipal bonds. Thus an interest rate of, say, 3 per cent, is equivalent to a 6 per cent coupon for persons in the 50 per cent tax bracket. "This is a real concession to municipalities," he added, "as it cuts borrowing costs quite drastically."
Mr. Coates also dealt with income tax returns in the United States and mentioned that the cost of care of children while the wife works is deductible to varying degrees-the lower the family income the greater the deduction allowable.
Although Mr. Coates did not say that certain recommendations are going to be made in the Carter commission report he did state that the absence of a capital gains tax in Canada is one of the reasons for the absence of risk capital in this country. That portion of the article reads as follows:
"The U.S. principle maintains that there is no capital and no income .. . there is only loss and gain," he explained.
"This brings up the question of which rate will you apply to certain gains, and what deductions will you allow for certain losses."
It is this recognition of possible loss that tends to make the U.S. citizen more venturesome. If he loses money on a venture, he may recoup some of it through tax deductions.
I suggest that part of the money which the Minister of Finance is seeking in order
The Budget-Mr. Robichaud
to buy back Canadian industry could come from the less venturesome Canadians if they were allowed to write off some of their investments in the event of loss.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I say that this has been one of the longest sessions I have attended since I became a member of parliament in 1958. I am pleased to have had the opportunity to give the government some of my views on problems that need attention, and when another opportunity presents itself I hope to deal with these matters further.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was not my intention to participate in this debate until the hon. member for Kings (Mr. McQuaid) invited me last Thursday to explain certain matters which he raised during the course of his remarks and expressed his disappointment that I was not in the house at the time. He referred to a press release which I issued on January 31 dealing with trap limits and licence control in a portion of lobster fishing
February 13, 1967

The Budget-Mr. Robichaud district 7B in Prince Edward Island. The hon. member said he was all in favour of the lobster trap limit and added that he was rather disappointed that the department had not gone all the way, meaning that the trap limit should have been applied to the whole of district 7B instead of being limited to a certain area of Prince Edward Island.
Last year a lobster trap limit was imposed in district 8 for the 1966 fall season, which opened on August 10 and closed on October 10. The district where the trap limit was imposed comprised part of Northumberland Strait, including Kent and Westmorland counties in New Brunswick, part of Cumberland county in Nova Scotia, as well as the county of Prince in Prince Edward Island. We are now assessing the results of this trap limit after a full season's operation. I am sorry the hon. member does not happen to be in his seat at the moment because I am sure he would have liked to listen to my remarks which I hope will clarify what he said on Thursday last.
On January 25 I had a meeting in my office with representations of the P.E.I. Fisheries Federation, including representatives of the fishermen, of the industry and of the co-operative groups. It was at the request of these gentlemen that I agreed to amend the regulations imposing for this year's spring season, a trap limit and some licence control in part of district 7B, in that portion which comprises the area from North Point to East Point, including all of the northeast coast of P.E.I. The gentlemen at that meeting told me this was a good area to make a dividing line. It was agreed that in that particular area the problem was most urgent and required immediate action, if possible.
[DOT] (6:20 p.m.)
I have stated already outside the house that it is our intention to carry out a survey of all lobster fishing areas during the next few months with the intention of introducing some controls and further trap limitations in other areas as soon as feasible. If in my announcement of January 31 I had included, as suggested by the hon. member for Kings, the whole of district 7B, this would have included also the southern part of Queens county and the southeastern part of Kings county in Prince Edward Island as well as part of Cumberland and all of Colchester, Pictou, Antigonish and Inverness counties in Nova Scotia.

I wish to warn the fishermen of all the maritime areas at this time that they can prepare now for further controlling action in respect of lobster fishing in 1968. I have stated before outside the house that we are not ready to impose trap limitations in all districts of the maritime provinces this year but that we wish to review fully the results of the application of the new regulation in district No. 8 last fall.
The present fishing activities are beyond what this resource can stand. The natural reproduction cannot support the accelerated and active fishing which now is taking place. If this most important natural resource is to be saved for future generations of fishermen, we will require the full co-operation of all fishermen presently engaged in the lobster fishing operation.
The hon. member also raised another question which concerns the Department of Fisheries. In 1964, in order to assist the inshore fishermen of the Atlantic provinces, I initiated a policy of federal subsidies for fishing boats from 35 feet to 45 feet in length. At that time I made clear that the purpose of this change was to obtain better boats for inshore fishermen and to help them diversify their operations. I also made it very clear that the purpose of this subsidy was not to increase the number of boats engaging in lobster fishing because this resource was already too extensively fished.
It would not be logical for the Department of Fisheries to approve the trap limitation, curtail licences, and then assist the lobster fishermen by means of subsidies to build additional boats. At the time of the announcement when we defined the purpose of the subsidy we made very clear that it was not the intention that this should apply to boats engaged exclusively in lobster fishing. In April of 1964, before making this announcement, I had a long discussion with representatives of the provincial governments of the Atlantic provinces. I also had a meeting in Charlottetown which was attended by the Minister of Fisheries for Prince Edward Island and his officials. So I do not think it would be fair for the hon. member for Kings to say, as he did, that these fishermen were not told that there would be strings attached to what they had to do to qualify for the subsidy in respect of the construction of boats in the 35 to 45 foot class.
The government of the province of Prince Edward Island and the Fishermen's Loan Board of that province were made well aware
February 13, 1967	COMMONS
of our intention. In fact, in July of 1964, following the meeting which took place at Charlottetown which was followed by a meeting between federal and provincial officials, I issued a press release which read in part as follows:
During the first few years of operations under the new regulations assistance to vessels under 45 feet in length will be limited to approved experimental designs. The Fishermen's Loan Boards in the provinces of New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia and Newfoundland, and the Minister of Industry and Commerce in the province of Quebec, will continue the direct administration of the new regulations. Close control over the design and specifications of craft eligible for assistance will be maintained by federal-provincial co-operation. This will include consideration of the numbers to be built each year, and their location, and the co-ordination of their construction with training projects designed to provide skilled manpower for a modern Atlantic fleet.
The hon. member also stated in his remarks that there were no prior consultations with the province of Prince Edward Island in so far as specifications were concerned. I wish to state that there was full consultation with officials of the Prince Edward Island government. In November of 1964 a special meeting took place in Charlottetown between officials of the federal Department of Fisheries and representatives of the Prince Edward Island government, including officials of the Fishermen's Loan Board, to discuss the subsidy program. Further meetings took place, and on July 12, 1965 an agreement was signed with the Fishermen's Loan Board of Prince Edward Island. The agreement was further amended in September of that year. I repeat that this agreement was signed after full discussion with the representatives of the province.
It is true that six applications which were presented by the Fishermen's Loan Board of Prince Edward Island were accepted as submitted because these met the requirements regarding construction standards as specified in the agreement. However, some time later, in the latter part of 1965, a total of 96 applications were received from the Fishermen's Loan Board of Prince Edward Island. It was found that these applications had not been screened according to the agreement with the Fishermen's Loan Board of that province. In December, 1965, just a month or two later, my deputy minister requested an immediate meeting with the deputy minister of fisheries for Prince Edward Island to discuss the problems relating to the subsidies. For reasons unknown to me, the then minister of fisheries for Prince Edward Island refused to agree to
The Budget-Mr. Robichaud such a meeting. It became evident to us that a full inspection of all boats for which applications had been received was necessary if public funds were to be protected. It was then that we made arrangements to have all boats inspected. This applied to all the Atlantic provinces, not only to Prince Edward Island. Immediately, between January and February of 1966, arrangements were made to proceed with this inspection.
After the inspection of these boats was completed, each individual case was discussed and reviewed with representatives of the fisheries department of Prince Edward Island at a meeting which took place in July of last year. It was agreed by officials of the federal Department of Fisheries and representatives of the Prince Edward Island government that a limited number of applications only was acceptable under the established criteria and that a certain number of boats needed some improvement before qualifying for the subsidy. It was also agreed that a larger number did not meet the requirements either of the Prince Edward Island Fishermen's Loan Board or of the federal government. Furthermore, we made clear to the representatives of that province that we were willing to pay the subsidy on the additional cost of the improvements which were required on 15 or more boats for which applications had been received provided the improvements were carried out as required by our agreement with the Fishermen's Loan Board of Prince Edward Island.
The inspection of the boats was made on the basis of the following specific policy and regulation:
-vessel to be of approved experimental design reflecting improvement over conventional types for the size class; vessel to meet provincial construction standards and Department of Transport regulations in so far as the latter apply; vessel to be registered with the Department of Transport; vessel to be adequately outfitted and equipped to show sufficient evidence of diversification capability over and above lobster fishing.
[DOT] (6:30 p.m.)
Therefore I want to make it very clear that the decision not to accept a number of applications was made only after full consultation with the government of the province of Prince Edward Island. We felt it was our responsibility and duty to protect the spending of public funds. Subsidies had to be paid according to established criteria and regulations.
Before I resume my seat I should like to take a minute or two to put on record certain
12978	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Robichaud facts relating to a matter which has been of great concern to me in recent years, and which has created quite a bit of interest in Canada and abroad. I refer to the sealing operation in the Gulf of St. Lawrence and on the front.
On December 9 in reply to a question addressed to me by the hon. member for Okana-gan-Revelstoke (Mr. Johnston) I stated in part that-
-we now have evidence that the film taken in 1964 was taken three days before the opening of the season. We have signed declarations by the participants that they were paid to perform certain operations not in accordance with regular practices in sealing.
I was not in a position to go into more details at that time. May I say that I have seen certain programs which were carried on television questioning that statement. Let me make it very clear that the film produced in 1964 by Artek Films Limited of Montreal for the C.B.C. French television network was partly staged. The cameramen participating in that filming admitted that it was filmed three days before the opening of the sealing season. The script was written by one Serge Deyglun who also voiced the script for the film. The same man was the one shown in the film shooting and wounding adult seals.
When I visited lies de la Madeleine last year I took this film along and it was shown at Cap aux Meules, lies de la Madeleine on Monday, March 7. The two cameramen who participated in the original filming were present and they admitted participation. They also admitted having shot a part of the film before the season opened. One of them admitted that he was the individual attempting to cut open a baby seal while it was still wriggling. He admitted that he was so disgusted he could not finish the job and had to ask a local fisherman, who was hired to participate in this operation, to finish the job for him.
Furthermore, a second film which was made in 1965 by Fleury Productions, which was shown on C.B.C television, and a portion of which was shown abroad, was composed of cuttings from the original film made in 1964, and part of an older film made by a former director of the Arctic biological station.
Following the showing of that film at lies de la Madeleine we obtained a sworn declaration from one of the fishermen who was engaged in the operation. I wish to put this declaration on the record, Mr. Speaker. I have it in translated form, and it states this:
I, the undersigned, Gustave A. Poirier, of Le Pre, lies de la Madeleine, declare having been engaged
[Mr. Robichaud.l
DEBATES	February 13, 1967
by a group of photographers, one of whom had a beard, and this was on or about March 3, 1964, to skin an adult seal for a film that they were taking at the time. I also solemnly declare before witnesses that I was asked to tease the said seal and not to use a club but only my knife for this operation. It is well known that in normal practice during a seal operation we use a club or a gaff to kill the seals before we skin them.
Gustave A. Poirier
Witnesses: P. A. Beauchesne Albert Delaney
Taken at Havre-aux-Maisons, March 12, 1966.
This is the type of film or extracts of film shown in Canada and abroad which have been so damaging to the image of this country. I am the first one to admit there have been abuses in seal hunting, but I think it fair to say that since 1964 we have taken a special interest in amending existing regulations in order to enforce methods of killing which are as humane as humanly possible. The new sealing regulations which will be in force this year will go a long way in this regard. I hope that during the next season, which opens on March 7 in the Gulf of St. Lawrence-

speechtext: Will the minister permit a question? Can he tell us whether action is contemplated against the companies which produced these films?

speechtext:
Unfortunately, because of the difficulty experienced in obtaining this information, two years passed before we were in a position to prove who the persons involved, were, and because of the regulations and existing laws no action could be taken against those who participated. We are amending these regulations in order to change the situation in respect of further actions of this kind.
Following this year's amendments sealing will be defined and will include all phases of the operation, from hunting to the transportation of pelts. Fisheries officers will be present aboard every sealer operation in the gulf and an officer will be present at every landing point of aircraft and helicopter. These points will be specified in advance, and in this way we will be able to control the quotas which we have imposed. Every hunter will be required to carry a special licence and wear an identification which will be issued with the licence.
Today I sent a circular to the owners of all large vessels operating in the gulf reminding them of their responsibilities and our intention to apply the regulations to the letter of the law. I hope the result will be the prevention of inhumane methods of killing seals.
February 13, 1967	COMMONS
Last year all the S.P.C.A. officials and veterinarians who attended the operations agreed that the most efficient and humane method of killing the seals was with a hardwood club. Some of them brought their own types of weapons, but in the final analysis they agreed that the hardwood club was the best weapon.
This year we have specified that every hunter will have to carry a hardwood club not less than 24 inches nor more than 30 inches in length, and not less than two inches in diameter. This year we have chartered four helicopters to carry the extra fisheries officers to the various ice flows in an attempt to control this operation and enforce the regulations. Many people are inclined to believe that this operation takes place on many fronts. That is not so. It takes place normally on a limited front, because the herds are together drifting with the ice.
During a survey last year 1,250,000 adult seals were spotted on the ice. In designing our regulations we must consider the fact that during periods before and after breeding or whelping these adult seals in the Gulf of St. Lawrence consume 15 pounds of fish each per day. When we are reminded of the quantity of fish that over a million seals would consume in one day, we also have to take into consideration the human aspect of this operation; we have to consider the fishermen from Newfoundland, Magdalen Islands, Prince Edward Island and the north shore of the St. Lawrence who are engaged in this operation. We also have to consider the some 40,000 fishermen from the Atlantic provinces who derive their livelihood from the fishery resources of the Gulf of St. Lawrence.

speechtext: I understand that there has been some kind of controversy about the value of the sealing industry. Could the minister place on the record any information with regard to that matter? It has been said that the value of this industry is so insignificant that we should completely eliminate the killing of seals.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I was just coming to that very point, Mr. Speaker. I am glad the hon. member has reminded me of it, but I was just coming to it. This kind of statement has been
The Budget-Mr. Robichaud made by people who have been accepted in this house as being responsible. The statement has been made in connection with the sealing operation, particularly by those who have been insisting upon its complete abolition, that the total value of seals to the sealers and landsmen is in the vicinity of $180,000 a year, and sometimes it has been said it is $300,000 a year.
I have the most recent figures. Last year the total landed value of seals during the seven weeks season was $1,889,121. This was during a period when there was no other type of revenue for the fishermen; they could not engage in fishing operations because of drifting ice. It is a period in which they are given the opportunity to earn a few dollars, perhaps enough to buy fishing gear and equipment for the fishing season which opens a month or two later. With regard to those who have been reported as earning $200 or $300 during the season, I would point out that those engaged in the large sealers as crew members earned from $1,100 to $1,300 during the sealing season last year. This information comes to me from two of the operators. I felt, Mr. Speaker, that these statements should be placed on the record. I want to clearly express my concern for this operation. It is my intention to impose regulations that will prevent any inhumane methods of killing in the operation, but I believe it is my responsibility to allow the sealing operation to continue.
We have also been criticized for not doing anything in the area called the "front" in which foreign sealers operate. We have succeeded in having the Norwegians agree not to fish in the Gulf of St. Lawrence and to allow us to enforce in full the existing regulations. We have also succeeded in having the sealing operation brought under the protocol of the International Convention of the North Atlantic Fisheries. This was achieved at a meeting which took place in Madrid in June of last year. It was agreed that the sealing operation would be accepted under the protocol of ICNAF. This again was followed by a meeting in Copenhagen, I believe, around the middle of October at which further steps were taken in this regard. Agreement was reached on an abstention of hunting during the breeding and whelping season and limited hunting seasons were accepted. This is a step forward. We hope at the next meeting, which will take place in Boston this year, we will be able to get these countries to accept further regulations so we can fully control this operation.

Mr. Speaker, it is my duty to join in the budget debate at this time because there are a number of topics that I wish to discuss. I bring most of them to the attention of the house because of the attitudes of this government, because of the lack of action of the government in some cases, and in other instances because of certain decisions they have made which are adverse to the welfare of the citizens concerned. Last Thursday evening in the division vote taken as a result of the amendment put forward by the official opposition, the government was sustained by only 12 votes. I was pleased to see all the opposition, and some independents, signifying their disapproval of the government's actions and policies.
[DOT] (6:50 p.m.)
The budget, since it represents the policy exemplified by the chief function of government, that of levying taxes, reflects not only the political but the administrative image of those to whom the people have given power. As reflected in the division last Thursday evening, to which I have referred, 60 per cent of the Canadian people do not approve of this government's policies and actions. I wish to commend the hon. member for York East (Mr. Otto) for the speech he made last Wednesday in which he severely criticized the administration for what amounts to its ineptitude, and its paralysis in the face of certain serious national situations. It is obvious that in order not to be too critical of his own party he dubbed it "a government of innocents", "a naive government that fails to face the realities of life".
Mr. Speaker, I submit that there is no room in Canada, big as it is, and even in its centennial year, for a government of this kind. The hon. member for York East is quite correct
February 13, 1967	COMMONS
when he warns his own party and its shaky administration in the following words:
It might be said that with our good intentions we may even be paving the road to oblivion.
I am not using his words to embarrass the hon. member for York East. On the contrary,
I think he is a man who stands on his own feet in this house and who voices strong, well founded and firm opinions.
I know that the people of this country at this time deplore the many failures which have taken place in several of our finance and insurance companies. Many arguments have been advanced here on this topic. I have received letters from people who have recently lost their investments. One of the powers given to the federal government by the British North America Act is the control of banking. That control should extend to all financial institutions. This government has recently taken umbrage as a result of criticism levelled at it in this regard, and when criticized they have iced the puck into the provincial end of the rink. I submit that federal authority over all finance is a prime necessity in this country, and the government should be the first and most important overseer, ensuring the rectitude of all finance across this land.
I have here a letter that I was most shocked to receive in December from lifelong friends, in which they tell me about having lost their entire savings of over $11,000 in the Prudential Finance Corporation fiasco.
I wish to state that in my opinion the federal government is as much responsible as the provincial governments, if not more so, for allowing this financial crime to occur. There is evidence that even as far back as 1956 suspicion as to the soundness of this company had been voiced. The reason that I place blame on the federal government is that they have not had the courage to place the securities exchange rules under federal jurisdiction. The past loose arrangement was probably satisfactory 100 years ago or even 50 years ago, when the stock market did not play such a vital role in our economic life. Since the government is trying to entice Canadians to invest in equity shares it is its prime duty to take over jurisdiction of all stock market operations and investments, similar to the ill-fated one made by my unfortunate friends, and to place them securely under strict regulations, despite the protests
The Budget-Mr. Alkenbrack of any other level of government. In my opinion a government that has not had the courage to do this must accept full blame for consequences, such as the Prudential Finance Corporation disaster and other recent instances.
We have heard some talk of suggested forms of remuneration to these unfortunate investors, but I think that as usual the government has no policy regarding this embarrassing question. It is both ominous and ironic that Canada, with all her apparent prosperity, is experiencing so many bankruptcies and instances of financial irresponsibility and lawlessness. Of course the government has brought a lot of its troubles upon itself because of its reckless method of vote getting in the last couple of elections. If the government, through its policies, will prostitute and weaken federal authority by toadying to the clamour of one province or any group of provinces, it must then seem to be patronizing in part the petulance of all of them.
Since this Liberal government came to power there has been a marked and ominous eroding of federal power at an alarming rate unknown in former years. Part of the reason for this is that the present administration has not earned the confidence of the people. Canadian people as a whole are indifferent to this administration because it has not been either responsive or responsible to their needs. The Liberal party has masqueraded too long as a pretended agent of all things to all people.
We know in ordinary life that we cannot assume such a role successfully. Let us take for example the government's attitude with regard to their own self-espoused policies on bilingualism and biculturalism. I warned the people of Quebec last year in a speech here dealing with the policies of the Prime Minister in this regard. I told them to put no trust in liberalism, and that they would regret the day that they did. You have noticed, Mr. Speaker, that only one month ago the majority of the Liberal convention in Quebec voted to support bilingualism and biculturalism in the rest of Canada, but endorsed unilingual-ism and monoculturalism only and exclusively in Quebec. Is this the way to unite our nation? Mr. Speaker, I suggest that you agree with me when I say no, this is not the way to unite Canada, even in its gala centennial year.
February 13, 1967

Mr. Speaker, at the time the house rose for dinner I was about to bring up a matter pertaining to the employment of firefighters in the armed services in my constituency and the unfair manner in which this government advertises for and hires firefighters and other personnel for Department of National Defence installations in Prince Edward county, namely the Mountain View airport and Camp Picton. The competition for the most recent openings for firefighters at Mountain View air station was first opened to Prince Edward county residents only. Later this was changed, and the competition was opened to residents of Trenton, Belleville and other points on the mainland.
The final results of the competition were that none of the applicants from Prince Edward county was considered or hired. The Civil Service Commission sets itself up as being an objective, non-political organization to serve all the people of Canada. However, they too are obviously tainted with Liberalism and, in this case, with the desire of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer) to placate some of his disgruntled servicemen at Trenton. Two of the successful applicants for these jobs are air force personnel due for retirement within two or three years.
I have here, Mr. Speaker, two brief letters from two of the unsuccessful applicants, both residents of Prince Edward county, both qualified, and who have been discriminated against by the government and this supine, co-operative Civil Service Commission. The first letter I wish to put on the record reads as follows:
In October 1966 a notice of a position as firefighter, Department of National Defence, for Mountain View, Ontario, was posted. The position was open to Trenton, Belleville and Prince Edward residents. Then in November another notice appeared in the post office for the same position but stated Prince Edward residents only. Then, in December another notice was posted. It was then open to the residents of Prince Edward county, Ontario, Mountain View, Ontario and Trenton, Ontario and locations.
I myself applied on all three notices and qualified. Then on January 9, 1967 a competition was held at 6 RD Trenton. The board consisted of three air

force officers and the civilian C.P.O. As to date I have not received any notice of my standing on competition, but four men have been notified by phone they have the positions.
This is a photostat copy, and it is a little dim in places.
Not one of these men are residents of Prince Edward county. Two are from the town of Trenton and two are air force personnel. These men are up for retirement within two and a half to three years. They applied for release from the service where they are employed as firefighters with the understanding that if they did not get the job at Mountain View they could stay in the service and finish out their service time. One of the servicemen that has been rewarded the position will receive a pension in the neighbourhood of $300 a month, and to add more, these servicemen start at top rate where other men start at the same job at the bottom and take three years to get top rate.
I, myself, am a veteran.
He gives his service number here, but I shall not reveal it.
I joined the army in 1952 and was honourably released in 1955. During my three years I served with Canadian army in Korea for 13 months. My personal feeling is that while Prince Edward has not too much industry, surely when there is an opening of any job class, a man from the county should be given first choice for work to be performed in the county.
Now, the other letter reads as follows:
Air force personnel with two or more years to go on retirement will receive jobs at Mountain View. Two other civilians living north of Trenton will be coming to work at Mountain View. They are volunteer firefighters in their own area. One service person retiring on pension with considerable time on enlistment is to receive one of the jobs. The other service person, not a resident of the county, also has enlisted time remaining but is retiring on full pension to take a job as a firefighter at Mountain View. The civilian personnel receiving jobs as firefighters at Mountain View are not residents in the county but are living at considerable distance from Mountain View and holding jobs in their respective areas. There are a number of applicants from the county who I feel have the adequate education, age and health standards to fill these vacancies.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
These letters are from two of the applicants who felt so hurt by this treatment that they took the trouble to write to me. There are many more applicants from Prince Edward county who feel likewise but have not written. Some of them have phoned me regarding this injustice.
Now the harm has been done. These rejected applicants ask nothing more from this government. They do not expect to be hired for the job, because by this time the government's pets in Trenton have received the nod from officialdom. The government is desperate in its efforts to try to retain electoral
February 13, 1967

support in the town of Trenton and at the Trenton air station. This has been dwindling away and Liberalism is finished at Trenton. A drowning man will grasp at a straw, Mr. Speaker.
In closing this incident 1 would ask the government please to be good enough to show enough manners to write the unsuccessful applicants for this position, who live in Prince Edward county, to thank them for taking the trouble to apply, and give them a reasonable explanation, if possible as to why they were unsuccessful.
Next, Mr. Speaker, I wish to make reference to the dairy industry, which is so important to our part of the country. As a result of representations from the official opposition, and other members in this house, certain legislation was brought about last autumn that implemented a justifiable and deserved improvement in the price of milk paid to the farmers of Canada. I told the house at the time that even that increase, with all its merit, was too little and too late.
The rapid escalation of all farm overhead and of the price of all the things that the farmer and milk producer has to buy has wiped out the economic benefits of the last increase in the federal subsidy. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Greene) has said that milk producers must look elsewhere than to government for any further benefits, or for any further economic stabilization of their industry. I am sure you will agree with me, Mr. Speaker, that such a statement is far too final and inadequate. It is a statement that ill becomes a minister in whose authority rests the economic and physical welfare of such a great industry as the milk producing industry.
What the minister has said in effect reveals his thinking concerning this problem. It is this: "Don't bother me any more. I gave you $4 and some odd cents per hundred for milk. You should now be satisfied. I am not a farmer, but as an Ottawa Valley lawyer I should know what is sufficient and good for you."
I am still quoting the obvious thoughts of the minister, Mr. Speaker. He must be saying to himself: "Now look somewhere else. Look to the markets for any further benefits that might save you from bankruptcy."
It is now common knowledge, Mr. Speaker, that every year, right across this country farmers are turning away from the production of milk at an alarming rate. Some 2,000 sold out their herds and quit last year in the province of Ontario alone. If this trend and

The Budget-Mr. Alkenbrack the lack of interest now shown by the Minister of Agriculture continues, one of these mornings he, and all the milk consumers for that matter, will open the front door and there will be no bottle of milk there. Then there will be hell to pay. The government will unjustly blame the farmers for all our troubles.
We read of the great days of the past, the 1880's, the 1890's, of the days when that giant cheese was produced at Perth and shipped to London for a famous world's fair of the past. The milk and cheese production figures of those days were many times what they are now. Moreover the powdered milk industry did not exist at that time. Much of the world population today is starving and we could be feeding them. But no, we sit here in our imagined affluence and opulence and ask a little group of islands, a few dots on the map in the south Pacific ocean, to supply us with butter. How ridiculous can the situation get, Mr. Speaker?
Yes, Mr. Speaker, it is true that in all phases of farm production except in the production of wheat and western grains we have seen better and more productive days. Canada as a nation today in her industrial choice is personified in the hymn:	"Lead Kindly
Light", where the pilgrim says:
I loved the garish day in spite of tears;
Pride ruled my will,
Remembering not past years.
Yes, the gaudy and showy United States standard of living, and its standard of commerce have lured the Canadian people to its luminescence. It has lured us away from our primary industries, one of which is dairy production, and placed us to a large part in the uncertain economy of secondary industries and manufacturing, much of which cannot compete successfully with countries like the United States, Japan and countries in central Europe.
I ask the house this question, Mr. Speaker: Are we too proud to continue to conduct an honourable primary industry when, with more assistance from the very people who must have dairy products, the dairy industry, both the production and the processing parts thereof could flourish and compete with the whole world, as they should, with the production potential that is latent here in Canada?
To go further, Mr. Speaker, I am sorry to state that hand in hand with the lack of interest shown by this government in the dairy industry we have another department, the Department of National Health and
February 13, 1967

The Budget-Mr. Alkenbrack Welfare which, through the Food and Drugs Act is also putting some farmers out of business. As I come to this point, Mr. Speaker, I wish to state-and I am sure that this opinion is shared by every member in the house-that there must be certain standards of purity and cleanliness in all our food products, including milk. And if the bacteria count or the sediment sample of a farmer's milk production exceeds a certain minimum, the milk should be refused access to the market and should not be processed for human consumption.
In this regard I wish to protest strongly against the methods used by the Belleville office of the food and drug division of the Department of National Health and Welfare. They are far too high-handed and autocratic.
I have received many complaints from milk producers in Prince Edward county whom these officials have hailed into court and prosecuted.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
These government inspectors, it seems, do not come into the farm premises, but work a cloak-and-dagger game, a gestapo game along the road. The department allows its inspectors to take samples of milk somewhere along the road or at the factory after the milk leaves the farm. I am told by reliable sources that they do not have the fortitude to go into the farm and present their credentials and take a sample of the milk from the milk can at the farm, as they ought to, but instead have developed a habit of lying in wait along the road somewhere between the farm and the factory. They stop the milk truck and take the samples at a time and place unknown to the producers of the milk. This is nothing but a sneaky, despicable, bureaucratic practice. Although the cans are numbered there is a high chance of error in determining what sample came from what can; I would remind hon. members that the interior of a completely enclosed milk-hauling truck is dark, which does not make identification easy. I strongly recommend to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen) that the present practices of his inspectors in connection with milk sampling and the high-handed manner in which they are treating the farmers of Prince Edward county be stopped.
I wish to point out, Mr. Speaker, that in every case I mention when milk has been condemned by the food and drug office it has subsequently been processed for human consumption. Nevertheless several Prince Edward farmers have been fined $100 each, plus costs, for producing this same low quality


milk, and yet this milk was processed along with the approved milk.
Apparently the samples are sent to Toronto. Bacteria counts show a rapid increase on the way. Are the results obtained in government inspection laboratories always reliable and truthful? I strongly doubt it, under certain circumstances I have mentioned. Samples should be taken at the farm and analysed locally.
One farmer was hauled into court last week at Picton. He obeyed his summons, appeared, and pleaded not guilty. The government then refused to go ahead with the case and had it remanded for a week on the ground that the evidence was not quite in shape. Do these officials think farmers have nothing to do but appear in court periodically for one and the same alleged offence? I would think that whatever evidence the government had would have been ready for presentation, since the Crown had had this evidence since last September 14, the date of the farmer's alleged offence against the act.
I am not saying there is no need for inspection. Certainly, we must have milk inspection, but not by the methods which are now being used. Then again, Mr. Speaker, I submit that a fine of $100 for the production of allegedly inferior milk which the government permits to be processed, and which is used and consumed by the people of Canada-yes, and exported abroad-is too severe a penalty. The money might better be used for the installation of more sanitary conveniences in the milk-producing industry-I refer to bulk tanks, milk transfers and improved stabling conditions. The department should be making grants of up to 40 per cent of the cost of such improvement to farmers who are willing to enter and stay in the milk production industry. In order to build this industry, to guard against its imminent extinction and to assure the attainment of the national stature which it deserves, the government should be giving it the assistance which I have outlined, instead of adding to its local problems.

During the debate last Friday, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Queens (Mr. Macquarrie) deplored the fact that, unfortunately, there were not as many opportunities to deal with external affairs problems in this house as there should be.
While I do not necessarily agree with his other views, I must also admit that these opportunities are very few indeed and time

February 13, 1967
The Budget-Mr. Duh6 and not with the North Atlantic council composed of national representatives who should be seeking an agreement to adopt a common position on a request or a study prepared by the assembly.
Mr. Speaker, our Canadian statesmen never hesitated to show their faith in the Atlantic alliance. I think this is a splendid opportunity to prove that we wish to strengthen the political ties uniting the Atlantic community. If NATO is to survive, it must adapt itself realistically to the present situation and become much more than a defensive military alliance. It must broaden its base and become an economic and political alliance.
I think that all right-thinking people today, all those who truly want peace in the world, are glad to see the gradual lessening of tension between East and West. Without weakening our defensive structure, we should, I think, explore every possibility of improving the political climate between the NATO countries and those of the Warsaw Pact.
Under the circumstances, the conference held last November recommended that the North Atlantic Council take definite steps toward establishing good relations with Eastern Europe on the economic, political and cultural level.
The NATO Assembly is aware that the main task of the Organization is always to ensure that security and integrity are maintained in the free countries of the West. However, it asks that a serious study be made of the advisability of organizing unofficial meetings with the representatives of the assemblies of the Eastern European countries.
In my capacity as Chairman of the Assembly, I intend to communicate to this effect with the competent authorities of the 15 countries of NATO and the eight countries of the Warsaw Pact in order to sound out their reactions.
I hope that parliament and the government of Canada will heartily support such an initiative that can only contribute to easing the international situation and to the peace of the world.
During this conference, several delegates from other countries belonging to the Alliance came to see the Canadian parliamentarians and told us they would be happy to hold the next conference in Canada. Besides, upon his return to Canada, the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) asked, On November 24, a question to that effect of

the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson). There are many factors in favour of such a proposal.
First, it will be the first time the conference will sit under the name of the North Atlantic Assembly. Considering the fact that Canadian statesmen have greatly contributed to the birth of the NATO concept and the first president of the conference was a Canadian, people naturally look to Canada.
Speaking of the first president, I must avail myself of this opportunity to pay tribute to Senator Wishart Robertson, of Nova Scotia, who has now retired. This gentleman has acquired abroad a very enviable reputation which will outlive him.
The centennial celebrations, especially Expo in Montreal represent a great attraction for the parliamentarians of the other 14 countries of the alliance. It is in 1967 that people from abroad will see us in our most favourable light, and in our finest array. Moreover, Canada has yet to host the conference.
I feel our prestige abroad could only be enhanced by the presence of so distinguished a group during our centennial. Unfortunately, it seems that due to the extra activities in Canada this year, this is practically impossible. Another argument deserves consideration. Holding the first meeting of the assembly in the very headquarters of NATO at Porte Dauphine in Paris will prove the interdependence between the NATO assembly and council.
Let us only hope that the headquarters at Porte Dauphine will still be accessible for the last meeting before the move to Belgium.
I also hope that Canada may be in a position to invite the assembly to sit in Ottawa in the near future.
Our delegates to the conference noticed the excellent reputation our country enjoys abroad. Of course, ours is not the prestige of a great power. It is rather a matter of friendship and respect our allies feel toward a young industrial nation which does not aspire to domination but wishes to contribute toward the development of sound and constructive international relations.
Mr. Speaker, we must continue to make the best of that favourable situation to help others while helping ourselves.
External aid is one of the most powerful instruments of our international policy. I feel that the great majority of Canadians agree that external aid is amply justified from a humanitarian point of view since it answers
February 13, 1967

the basic principle of charity. There is no doubt, either, that external aid is fully justified from an economic point of view since it creates employment at home and paves the way for future markets.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)

In his recent book titled "A Samaritan State", Keith Spicer had this to conclude about Canadian external aid:
A meaningful global judgment on the numerous activities of Canada's aid program seems objectively impossible. It is easy enough to assess each kind of aid separately on its own merits. But there exists no universally accepted standard for evaluating a total program; criteria purporting to serve this function are invariably tainted with the narrow prejudices of single disciplines: economics, politics or sociology.
Until adequate methods of measurement are found, general judgment cannot really reach beyond the subjective and impressionistic. Has Canadian aid been "successful" or "effective"? The question is no more manageable than one asking whether a person "likes" a certain country. One can scarcely do more, in a few words, than reply vaguely that Canada's aid, compared with that of other large donors, appears to have been consistently high in quality, and free of spectacular waste or scandal; its administration has grown from makeshift to mediocre, then, since about 1960, to a steady competence tarnished only by a cramping weakness in the field and by understaffing at home. Finally, its operations have enabled Canada to forge with several developing countries relations of intimacy, trust and fairly stable understanding. Any more precise opinions must be sought in detailed criticism of each type of aid taken by itself.
Mr. Spicer has many interesting proposals under the heading "Machinery of Policy Review", one of which I should like to draw to the attention of the government. I quote from page 248:
The crucial arena of policy co-ordination is, of course, the cabinet. A cabinet committee reflecting the whole range of foreign policy instruments would have to include the Prime Minister as chairman, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the ministers of National Defence, Manpower, Trade and Commerce, Finance and (for cultural diplomacy) the Secretary of State. Attached to this group of ministers would be a permanent interdepartmental committee of high civil servants, sometimes including, for the Secretary of State, representatives of the C.B.C., the National Film Board and the Canada Council. Both these committees would operate in the customary fashion, civil servants advising, ministers deciding.

Mr. Speaker, I have thus made some remarks as regards our foreign policy and external aid.
In closing, I feel duty bound to state that my remarks and suggestions set out to be constructive. I have never had to be ashamed
The Budget-Mr. Douglas of our international role. I simply want this role to keep growing at the same pace as our national development and destiny.

Mr. Speaker, my sole reason for taking part in this debate is to make a few comments regarding the speech made this afternoon by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) in connection with the unhappy state of affairs in Viet Nam. I must say that in some ways it was a pathetic speech, because it was so apparent that the minister's heart was not in it. I have had the privilege of knowing the minister for a long time. He and I entered parliament in the same election. I have a very high personal regard for him. I believe him to be a man of peace and deep sensitivity. I am sure there were many things he would have liked to say this afternoon which he did not say.
At least the speech made by the minister was an improvement over some other speeches he has made in connection with Viet Nam, because in the past he has mainly spent his time defending the United States policies in Viet Nam. Today he delivered an apologia for Canada doing nothing. We witnessed today the Secretary of State for External Affairs, like Pontius Pilate of old, publicly washing his hands of all responsibility. The minister today contented himself with avowing the government's good intentions and disavowing any actions which might give effect to those intentions.
The minister told us that Canada could not do very much in this unfortunate situation because we are a member of the International Control Commission, we are a neutral, we are a non-combatant, and the best thing for Canada and for him to do is just not rock the boat. I should like to point out, Mr. Speaker, that in the first place Canada's neutrality has not in the past prevented the minister from defending United States policies in Viet Nam. I can recall when the people who were protesting against the war in Viet Nam were parading in front of the parliament buildings the minister and his aide were handing out mimeographed copies of a brief which was a rehash of the United States white paper. I can remember also some of the speeches the minister made in this house in which he defended the domino theory with as much enthusiasm and eloquence as John Foster Dulles ever managed to muster.
I should like to refer the house to Hansard of April 2, 1965 at page 13108 where the
February 13, 1987

The Budget-Mr. Douglas Secretary of State for External Affairs said this:
Mr. Chairman, Viet Nam is a test case; I suggest that if the North Vietnamese aggression with Chinese connivance succeeds, it will only be a matter of time before the next victim is selected. The issue then concerns the security, integrity and independence of small nations, not only in Asia but all over the world. If the United States were to leave Viet Nam at the present time, what would happen to that country? What would happen to Burma? What would happen to India, a Commonwealth country? What would happen to Malaysia, a Commonwealth country? What would happen to the Philippines, and what would happen to those island countries of Australia and New Zealand? What would be the position of Japan? These are considerations that must be borne in mind by anyone who simplifies the problem in the way that my friend, the hon. member for Kootenay West, has sought to simplify this complicated problem.
Well, Mr. Speaker, that does not sound very neutral. That sounds to me like a very spirited defence of United States intervention in Viet Nam. Nor has our membership in the International Control Commission prevented Canada selling some $300 million worth of war materials a year to the United States, with no assurance whatsoever that it is not being used in an undeclared war upon a small country in southeast Asia.
Would my hon. friend permit me to ask whether he said we were selling $300 million worth of equipment to Viet Nam?

No. I said we are selling to the United States some $300 million worth of war materials, and we have no guarantee at all that none of that material is going to the war in Viet Nam. If the minister could give us the assurance that it is not going there I would be one of the happiest persons in this house. I am sure the minister cannot give that assurance, and I shall be dealing with that matter later, because I think the Canadian government has tried to get that assurance but has been refused.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
Canada is not in a peculiar position in that it is a neutral, a non-combatant or a member of the International Control Commission. Other countries which are neutral have spoken out. The government of France has expressed its opinion on what is happening in Viet Nam. India, which is also a member of the International Control Commission and much more dependant on United States' good will than is Canada, has spoken out. The Prime Minister of India, Indira Gandhi, within the last ten days has made a personal
[Mr. Douglas.!

appeal to President Johnson of the United States to cease the bombing of North Viet Nam. Sweden, which has always prided itself as a neutral, has not only spoken out against the bombing of North Viet Nam, but has halted the shipment of any war materials to the United States until such time as the war in Viet Nam is brought to an end.
Therefore the fact that we are a neutral and a member of the International Control Commission, it seems to me, does not justify for one moment the minister's contention that Canada must be silent, that Canada must be inactive and that Canada instead of speaking out should take refuge in what he calls quiet diplomacy. We are not talking about some dispute over a boundary. When we are discussing the Viet Nam issue we are discussing the greatest moral issue of our time. As I have said before, in the opinion of the members of this party the bombing of North Viet Nam is legally indefensible and morally inexcusable. What is happening in Viet Nam is shocking the conscience of the world more than anything that has happened since Hitler tried to exterminate the Jews in Europe. The bombing not only of military targets but civilians, now proven beyond any shadow of a doubt, has caused millions of people in the world to question this disastrous military conflict. The use of anti-personnel bombs and the use of napalm has made the war in Viet Nam a bloody and barbaric incident that has no equal in our time.
This is why his Holiness Pope Paul VI has spoken out in protest and has pleaded for the cessation of the bombing; this is why the World Council of Churches has pleaded for the cessation of bombing and for negotiations, and this is why the Secretary General of the United Nations, the world's foremost civil servant, has called for a halt to the bombing and the beginning of negotiations. Scientists, university faculties and university students all around the world have pleaded with the government of the United States to stop the bombing in the hope that this will be the first step toward finding a solution to the trouble in Viet Nam.
In today's Globe and Mail there appeared an article entitled "End Ties with NORAD, Student Liberals Urge", which states in part:
A ban on sales of Canadian weapons to the United States for the duration of the Viet Nam war and withdrawal next year from the U.S.-Canada North American Air Defence Command were called for Saturday by the Canadian University Liberal Federation.
February 13, 1967	COMMONS DEBATES
It then states:
The original resolution called for a halt to bombing of North Viet Nam, recognition of the National Liberation Front as a legitimate political group in the south and de-escalation of military operations and gradual withdrawal of U.S. forces.
That is the attitude of university students in Canada who belong to the Liberal party. After reading that report this morning I am not surprised that the minister felt it was incumbent upon him to make a statement this afternoon regarding government policy in respect of Viet Nam. The minister must be aware that Canadians, like people the world over, are aroused by what is happening in this barbaric war, the effect it is having on the people who live there, the consequence that may follow in escalating into a major war, and the long term effect it will have in building up barriers between the oriental people and the people of the western world. People are aroused; Canadians are aroused and I want to tell the minister that it will take more than verbal soporifics and platitudinous declarations to quiet their fears and their concerns.
It is recognized by almost everyone that the first essential step in finding a solution to the Viet Nam situation is to bring about a halt in the bombing of North Viet Nam. This is one obstacle which must be resolved before any progress can be made. This was apparent when the representative of the North Vietnamese government located in Paris made a statement a short time ago which was reported in the Globe and Mail on January 6. The report is from Paris, by Richard E. Mooney, who says:
North Viet Nam's chief diplomatic representative in western Europe said yesterday that if the United States "definitively and unconditionally" stopped bombing his country, the Hanoi Government would "examine and study" U.S. proposals for negotiations.
This is one thing that must be done. Newspaper reports have indicated that as a result of the Warsaw discussions the United States and North Viet Nam came close to agreeing on negotiations. The Globe and Mail of February 2 carries a dispatch from the United Nations which states:
Diplomatic sources said yesterday that the United States and North Viet Nam agreed in early December to hold preliminary peace talks in Warsaw but U.S. bombings near Hanoi broke up the agreement.
The article also states:
They explained that that was because the United States has agreed to talk about some things North Viet Nam was especially interested in-such as the neutralization of South Viet Nam.

The discussions on a date first were discouraged, the sources said, when the U.S. bombs hit a Polish-built school for Vietnamese children in the Hanoi area Dec. 2. Still, they proceeded until the December 13-14 raids.
After that the discussions broke off. It is only human nature that it is difficult to get people together around a negotiation table when their homes are being destroyed and their wives and children are being killed by anti-personnel bombs.
The United States government had a similar experience when Mr. Goldberg went to the United Nations, and, with great fanfare, said that President Johnson was prepared to give the Secretary General U Thant, complete carte blanche and an unconditional free hand to work out any kind of agreement he could for negotiations. What happened when U Thant came back with a three-tiered proposal, first that the bombing of North Viet Nam come to a stop, second, that the National Liberation Front be allowed to sit at the bargaining table, and third, that eventually all foreign troops should be withdrawn and the principles of the Geneva accord put into effect? The United States government, which had said that U Thant had a free hand to work out any terms he wanted, gave a firm, negative response to the very first proposal, namely a halt to the bombing of North Viet Nam.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
During the past few days, in the city of London, Premier Kosygin and Prime Minister Wilson have been holding discussions. I am one of those who has been critical of these two countries, Great Britain and the Soviet union, who are joint chairmen of the International Control Commission, for their inactivity. I have expressed this criticism to Mr. Wilson. When our parliamentary delegation was in Moscow in the fall of 1965, I expressed the same view to Mr. Mikoyan, who was then president of the U.S.S.R. I think they could have done more than they have done. But at least in the past few days the representatives of these two great powers have been examining this problem and exploring some means by which negotiations could be commenced.
While these negotiations are still going on, the government of the United States has resumed the bombings that had been temporarily suspended during the lunar new year. If ever there was a piece of bad timing, surely this was it. I can well understand the sadness in the voice of the Secretary of State for External Affairs when he had to tell the
February 13, 19S7

The Budget-Mr. Douglas house this afternoon that the bombing had been resumed. I would imagine that if the discussions of Premier Kosygin and Prime Minister Wilson come to naught, the resumption of the bombings will certainly be a major factor in that result. The minister said this afternoon, in announcing that the bombings had been resumed, that the United States of course is only waiting for some minimal response in order to cease the bombings. I would like to know what kind of minimal response is required to persuade someone to stop doing something they have no right to do. What is the minimal response required? No one has spelled this out.
Some United States spokesmen, such as Dean Rusk, have said, stop the infiltration of men and supplies from the north to the south; but Secretary of Defence McNamara told the defence committee of the United States Congress within the last 10 days that there has been only a trickle of men and supplies since last June going from North to South Viet Nam. The fact is, as Walter Lippmann the dean of American commentators has pointed out, that the United States has never faced up to the major points which Secretary General U Thant placed before it:	first,
whether or not they are prepared to treat with the National Liberation Front, recognizing that they have a right to speak for some of the people of South Viet Nam and, second, whether or not they are prepared to grant the right of self-determination to the people of Viet Nam. Every time the President or one of his spokesmen talks about returning to the principles of the Geneva accord, they say at the same time that South Viet Nam must remain as a sovereign power-which of course is completely contrary to the principles of the Geneva accord, which says that the people of Viet Nam have the right to decide whether South Viet Nam will remain a sovereign power or whether it will be merged with North Viet Nam into one nation.
Walter Lippmann put it well in an article which appeared in the Montreal Gazette of January 12 last, when he said:
The real obstacle to a negotiated peace is a very substantial one. It is whether or not, on any terms that are practicable in the actual world, the United States would evacuate its military positions on the mainland of Southeast Asia.
That puts it in a nutshell. Does the United States eventually intend to withdraw from Southeast Asia, or does it intend to retain a military foothold, not only in Viet Nam where it has spent billions of dollars in military installations, but now in Thailand where it is

building up tremendous military forces? Negotiations will come to naught unless the United States is prepared, in all sincerity, to say that it will abide by the principle of the right of self-determination and allow the Vietnamese people to decide for themselves what government they want and whether they want the North and the South to coalesce and, if the people decide that, have the United States and all other foreign troops withdraw.
I was glad to hear the Secretary of State for External Affairs this afternoon say that the Canadian government is in favour of a return to the principles of the Geneva accord. Yet I would remind the minister that it is not too long ago, about a year and three quarters, that he told us in the external affairs committee that the government of South Viet Nam, because it had not signed the Geneva accord, was not bound by it.

Not legally bound. I think this is a preposterous interpretation, since the Republic of France signed, and France was the governing power at that time. But this is exactly the kind of political and legal legerdemain which is making it very difficult to get any negotiations under way.
I want to say that in the opinion of the members of the New Democratic Party the time for quiet diplomacy is over and the time for speaking out is here.

have done. The minister tells us that the intentions of the Canadian government are pacific. I have no doubt about that. I have no doubt about the minister's own intentions, because he is a man of peace. What I am questioning is their lack of courage in giving voice to their convictions. I am questioning the veil of silence which they have assumed at a time when, on a great moral issue, this government should be speaking out for the people of Canada.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
The minister said this afternoon that if we make any declaration that might be construed as being critical of those taking part in this unhappy war, this would close up channels and would prevent our being effective as a peacemaker. I suggest that we have had quiet diplomacy; it has gone on for several years, and nothing has come of it. Now we have reached the place where the world leaders are speaking out because they recognize that the time has come for action.
This afternoon the minister ridiculed the idea of having a resolution passed by parliament calling for the cessation of the bombing. Why should parliament not pass a resolution, as was suggested by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition. The minister said this would close doors. But it also might open eyes and open ears; it might strengthen the hand of those in the United States and in the United States government who are trying to persuade the United States government to change its policy. It might help those who are endeavouring to have a moderating influence on the hawks in the American administration and I think it would have an effect on the American public.
The American people know that we are a friendly people, that we like the Americans, that we visit back and forth, that we trade with them, and that in our culture, our language and our habits we are probably more like them than any other nation in the world. I think it would give them reason to pause and think, if they found that their friendly neighbour to the north had come to the place where they could no longer remain silent and that we are calling upon them, in the name of justice and humanity, to stop this barbarous bombing of a small undefended people in an undeclared war.
After all it is a rather new theory of liberalism that on moral issues one should not rock the boat. The great star of liberalism was William Ewart Gladstone. When he was

The Budget-Mr. Douglas an old man he came back from retirement to rouse the British people in moral protest against the atrocities of the Turks, and he did rouse them. I see no reason why on a moral issue that is much greater, that affects many more people and is a greater threat to the peace of the world, this government and this parliament should not speak out.
I think that Canada should have the courage at this time to say that we will not sell any armaments to the United States unless we have the assurance that those armaments will not be sent to Viet Nam. My information is that the Canadian government has already appealed to the United States government and asked for assurance that none of the $300 million worth of armaments we sell them each year will go to Viet Nam. My information is that that plea has been rejected, and certainly nothing that the minister said in answer to my question this afternoon-

As I was saying, Mr. Speaker, the answer that the minister gave this afternoon certainly does not convince me that my information is wrong. I think the United States government has refused to assure us that any of the arms we are selling them are not going to Viet Nam. We have been very strict in saying to the French that any uranium we sell to them must not go for military purposes, and I support the government in that. Why do we not do the same with reference to the sale of arms? The minister said that we signed a defence sharing agreement. Mr. Speaker, this is not defence. These are weapons for aggression, and we have a perfect right to say that if weapons which we are selling to the United States for purposes of defence are going to be used in a war of aggression, then we will not sell those weapons to them.
The minister said this afternoon that we received $300 million a year for these arms and that this is a very important item in our
