I will tell the minister the policy of this party. Our policy is that if the United States will not give us a firm commitment that none of these armaments which we are selling to them are going to the war in Viet Nam, then we should be prepared to abrogate that agreement. Because while a loss of $300 million in our trading position would be serious I am not prepared to get $300 million of trade, if it is at the price of the tears of mothers who have lost their children, and if it is to be at the cost of seeing villages annihilated and defenceless people killed.
I will close by saying that I cannot accept the minister's thesis that there is a difference between an individual's convictions and a government's declaration. The minister's thesis this afternoon was that, irrespective of what one may think personally, if one is a member of the government he must not express his opinions publicly. Mr. Speaker, most of the war and bloodshed that we have seen in our lifetime has come because of the cowardly silence of governments in days gone by. I was a member of this house when the Liberal government withdrew Dr. Riddell from the League of Nations because he dared to suggest oil sanctions against Mussolini-he was rocking the boat.
I stood in my place in this house and protested against the sale of copper, scrap iron and nickel to Japan when Japan invaded Manchuria. We were told we must not rock the boat, and this silence, this apathy and inaction has brought us again and again into the maelstrom of war.
1 say that the time has come when a government in a democracy must speak for the people of Canada, and I believe the majority of the people of Canada would want this government to speak out on their behalf, to speak out against what is happening in Viet Nam, to call upon this government to express on behalf of all Canadians our desire that the bombing of North Viet Nam cease, that negotiations begin on the basis of the Geneva agreement, and if we cannot get that assurance that the Canadian government will not sell armaments if they are destined for use in Viet Nam.

Mr. Speaker, every man and woman must live with his or her own conscience, and in this hour of crisis in the world this parliament has to speak out. Someone has said that the modern world is treading a tightrope between Utopia and cremation. Surely we can do our part to see that the world comes down on the side of Utopia and of human survival.

I think that the United States has done many fine things in giving leadership in the free world. I think of the Marshall plan. I think of the assistance which they gave militarily in Europe when the free world was threatened by Soviet aggression, and when they helped preserve the peace of the world. However, the leadership of the United States in the forties and fifties took place in a world in which we had a great communist, monolithic structure that was in danger of spreading across the world.
What has happened is that the world situation has changed, but United States foreign policy has not changed with it. This communist monolithic structure is fragmented today; the Soviet union and China are sparring with each other; the satellites of the Soviet union are demanding more and more independence; and with the detente in Europe, the danger of military aggression by the eastern powers has greatly receded.
Men like Senator Fulbright and George Kennon, men like the former United States ambassador to Japan, have all been appearing before the foreign relations committee of the United States, pointing out to them that we are facing a new situation. The situation we face today is, how can we mobilize all the nations of the world who want to preserve freedom and to work together for freedom. Taking the position the United States is taking, that of forcing a country to accept a military dictatorship because it may be anticommunist, is only going to incur their antipathy rather than win their friendship.

Now they are talking among themselves, Mr. Speaker. When they get a little handed back to them they do not like it, and they panic. They get all excited. They have not got their advisers around them from the universities, or their beatniks walking up and down-as they are busy walking up and down in front of the United States embassy tonight.
Why do not some of these hon. members suggest to the North Vietnamese that they co-operate a little more? This afternoon the minister of external affairs pointed out to the House of Commons that there is no doubt that President Johnson of the United States is in a mess. We all agree that this war should never have occurred. They would like to end the war. To the best of my knowledge the Americans are not warmongers by nature, and never have been. If they had we would not be here.
The important thing to remember is that all they have asked of the Viet Cong and the North Vietnamese is for some conciliation, for some indication that they are sincere in their desire to de-escalate the war. There has been a fair period of truce when no bombing in North Viet Nam has taken place. I share the same view as everyone else in this house, including the minister of external affairs, that we wish this pause would continue. But we must remember that American boys are dying, not Canadian, and they have to make the decision. We are trying to be a mediator.
This is a particularly difficult role that Canada has, along with Poland. It is a role that Sweden does not have and that France does not have. President de Gaulle can say what he likes about the United States: He
The Budget-Mr. Mackasey does not have the same responsibility that our Department of External Affairs has.
If we were to follow the suggestion made by the leader of the New Democratic Party tonight, we would pass a resolution which condemns the United States for bombing North Viet Nam. Are you looking for some more notes?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour

It is about time somebody stood up and let the Canadian people know what the happy little gang in the corner represents-not what they think they represent, but what they do represent. They represent socialism in its worst form. They represent anti-Americanism in its worst form. They had an opportunity to help the farmers of this country, and they helped them until it became an embarrassment, not to the farmers but to that party. So they then threw the farmers out and said they would support labour. Now the marriage to labour is getting a little embarrassing, especially to the New Democratic Party.
In this day and age of modem communication the members of the N.D.P. cannot walk into Quebec and say one thing to rival trade unions, and then go into Ontario and tell another group something else.

What about Saskatchewan? When the leader of the New Democratic Party

The Budget-Mr. Mackasey ran in Saskatchewan he could not even get elected from that province as a representative to the federal House of Commons. This reflects nothing against the integrity of the hon. gentleman, who is one of the more respected of the senior politicians of this country. It is what he represented-an outmoded way of life which held the province of Saskatchewan back for 20 years.
One has only to check the growth of population in Saskatchewan during the 16 years of socialist rule, and compare it with the growth of population in Manitoba, British Columbia and Alberta. During the recent pipe line debate we heard nothing but anti-American statements from them. We have heard nothing but antiAmerican statements in connection with the Viet Nam crisis. But the fact is that in Saskatchewan people had 16 years of socialism and chucked them out. It is not only the experience in countries like Sweden, with its strong central government, that we must consider in evaluating the socialists. Now they stand in this house and tell the minister of external affairs how he should handle foreign policy.
That is the right of every member of the House of Commons, and no one can take it away from the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas). But one would expect a man of his integrity, a man of his reputation and a man with his years of experience in the political arena to have made a positive, concrete speech offering suggestions to the minister, one which would have been sympathetic to his delicate role, and worthy of the leader of a party in the House of Commons. speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-POSSIBLE INCREASES IN CEILING AND BENEFIT RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Wednesday, February 8, as recorded at page 12797 of Hansard,
I put this question to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson):
In view of his statement this morning to the Canadian Labour Congress, that he shares the view that the ceiling and the benefit rates under the Unemployment Insurance Act should he raised, can he say whether or not this will be done this year?
The minister's reply was as follows:
Mr. Speaker, as I have already advised the house, this depends on the recommendations that might come from the Unemployment Insurance Commission, to which parliament has delegated certain responsibilities in this field. I can assure the hon. member that so far as the Minister of Labour is concerned, he meant sincerely what he said this morning and my views are well known. I hope we will receive those recommendations shortly.
Mr. Speaker, in a moment I wish to refer to the supplementary question I asked and the answer given to it. First may I say, however-and I say it with some fear and trepidation in view of the fact that the parliamentary secretary who probably will be answering me is in full flight tonight and there is no telling what he will do to me-that I have very seldom heard such a lame excuse for failing to act as the excuse that the Minister of Labour gave me last Wednesday. He said in effect that the government has to wait until it has a recommendation from the Unemployment Insurance Commission before it can raise the ceiling on the benefit rates set out in the Unemployment Insurance Act.
May I point out that these figures, both the ceiling and the benefit rates, are in the statute passed by parliament. Changes have been made from time to time over the years since 1940, but they have always been made by government bills amending the statute. I know of no case when this was done on any other initiative than that of the government itself. It is a lame excuse for the government now to say it cannot act on these matters until it gets a recommendation from a commission which, though provided for by parliament, has been appointed by the government.
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
The fact of the matter is that it is a period of eight years since the present benefit rates were fixed. They were fixed in 1959 at $27 per week maximum for a single person and $36 per week maximum for an unemployed person with dependants. During that period the Gill committee sat. It made a recommendation about five years ago that these figures should be raised respectively to $36 and $48. If the government wants a recommendation, it has received one from the Gill committee, although even those figures are now out of date.
If the parliamentary secretary will look up the act he will find there is a section in it which gives the governor in council the authority to ask the Unemployment Insurance Commission to ask the advisory committee to state its opinion on various matters including the ceiling and the benefit rates. That does not say that the government cannot bring the matter before parliament, even if the commission or the advisory committee has not made such a recommendation. As I suggest, in my experience in respect of this legislation decisions have been taken by the government and brought before parliament on the government's own responsibility.
I said a moment ago that I should like also to refer to the supplementary question I put to the minister last Wednesday, and his reply. My supplementary question was:
In view of the fact that the act permits the government to ask the commission for recommendations, has the government asked for such recommendation?
The minister's reply was:
Mr. Speaker, I have asked the chief commissioner to let me have his views and those of his fellow commissioners.
Please note that I asked the minister a question based on my reading of the act; had the government asked the commission, or had the governor in council passed an order in council requesting the commission to give its opinion. The minister's reply was that he personally had asked the chief commissioner personally to give him his views and the views of his fellow commissioners. Surely that is not carrying out the intent of the act, namely that there can be an official reference from the governor in council to the Unemployment Insurance Commission. This is based on a chat over a cup of coffee, if you please, which I suggest is quite out of keeping with the terms of the act.
13000	COMMONS DEBATES	February 13. 1967
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
This is the second time in the last two or three weeks I have raised this question during a late show. I hope I have made my point with the parliamentary secretary, whether I have made one or not with the minister, the department or the government.
This is a matter of government responsibility, and it is a lame excuse indeed to say the government has not had a recommendation from the Unemployment Insurance Commission because there has apparently not been a formal request by order in council. It is eight years since the present maximum rates were set. It is time to increase these rates, and certainly the increases must go even higher than those proposed by the Gill committee. I call upon the government not to use any more excuses but to act on this matter without further delay.

maintopic: HOUSING-ACCELERATION OF CONSTRUCTION IN SAGUENAY-LAKE ST. JOHN AREA
HOUSING-ACCELERATION OF CONSTRUCTION IN SAGUENAY-LAKE ST. JOHN AREA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as reported on page 12826 of Hansard for February 9, I asked the following question of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson):
Mr. Speaker, I wish to put a question to the Minister of Labour in connection with his statement to the house last January 30.
Can the minister tell the house whether he will recommend to the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation any increase in residential housing in Saguenay-Lake St. John?
Mr. Speaker, it is undeniable that there is throughout Canada a very acute housing shortage.
The authorities, federal and provincial, are asked to do something about the problem which comes under their jurisdiction. It seems that the complaints directed at them will get the representatives of the federal and provincial governments, the mayors and other city officials concerned moving.
It is unanimously agreed that adequate housing must be provided for each Canadian family but what has been done to prevent increases in the price of new houses, higher interest rates, higher prices for building materials and tools, higher salaries and higher taxes of all kinds? It is surely the responsibility of the governments and municipalities to cut their expenditures and taxes to bring down prices and interest rates because the higher interest rate on mortgages granted under the National Housing Act can only stimulate a certain kind of construction but not that of low rental housing.
In the realm of the Saguenay-Lake St. John, the crisis is especially due to the absence of salubrious, low-rent housing accommodation. Most industrialized towns in that area are facing the inhuman problem of slums where large families whose head is a small wage-earner are crowded. These families have a right to hope for better housing which would favour their self-achievement. In Chicoutimi, queen of the Saguenay, there is practically
February 13, 1967	COMMONS
no suitable houses at a cost in keeping with the budget of small wage-earners. There would be room for large apartment buildings in that municipality.
In Port Alfred, there is a trend to convert basements into apartments renting from $60 to $90 a month. I wonder whether they meet all the standards of hygiene and safety to which the public is entitled.
In the town of Jonquiere, a survey carried out in September 1966 shows that certain parts of the city are faced with the crucial problem of slums. It reveals that out of 967 houses, 403 are in a state of major disrepair and 123 others are absolutely untenantable.
Mr. Paul Tremblay, town clerk of Alma, county seat of the constitutency I represent here, comments that a housing crisis would surely develop in that community if the 25 units considered unsanitary and housing poor people were condemned.
I ask the minister to tell us what action he intends to take to remedy this serious problem affecting our area.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
maintopic: HOUSING-ACCELERATION OF CONSTRUCTION IN SAGUENAY-LAKE ST. JOHN AREA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the hon. member for Lac Saint-Jean for his concern about housing in his particular area of the province, and I would like to tell him also that, as I am sure he knows, this is essentially a provincial matter. I would like to tell him that last Monday or Tuesday I had the privilege of meeting the minister of municipal affairs for the province of Quebec, Hon. Paul Dozois, who indicated that one of the first pieces of legislation which the Quebec legislature intends to adopt in the very near future is the establishment of a Quebec housing corporation. As the hon. member no doubt is aware, most provinces across Canada have similar corporations dedicated to the eradication of slums, to urban renewal developments and to public housing in general.
I would suggest to the hon. member that the best way of proceeding to obtain what he wants, that is better housing for his district, is first to create a demand on the civic level from the various towns and municipalities which need this help, and second to send a formal indication adopted by the council to the minister of municipal affairs or to the Quebec housing corporation when it is established.

I agree with the conclusion of the hon. member that this is indeed one of the main problems facing Canada. I must point out to him, as one Quebecker to another, that this problem is provincial in jurisdiction; but this should be no impediment, particularly in view of the very cordial relations that exist between Quebec and Ottawa.
